item.title: Efficient classical simulation of Fermi-Hubbard models with Kramers symmetry
item.description: arXiv:2611.10039v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum Monte Carlo methods are widely used to solve quantum many-body problems. However, rigorous guarantees for their performance are poorly understood, especially for simulating interacting fermions. In this work, we develop a quantum Monte Carlo algorithm for a broad family of fermionic systems exhibiting Kramers time-reversal symmetry, and prove that their partition functions can be estimated in polynomial time. This family, which contains many important classes of Hubbard-type models, is known to both avoid the sign problem and obey a Lee-Yang zero-freeness theorem. Thus our results suggest that these two properties together may enable efficient classical algorithms for quantum many-body systems more broadly.
item.dc:creator: Chaithanya Rayudu, Jun Takahashi, Ojas Parekh, Andrew Zhao

item.title: Dynamic Edge Orientation on Low-Arboricity Graphs: Breaking the $\log n$ Barrier
item.description: arXiv:2611.10161v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the dynamic edge orientation problem introduced in a seminal 1999 paper by Brodal and Fagerberg: given a fully dynamic graph $G$ with arboricity bounded by $\alpha$, maintain an orientation on $G$'s edges so every vertex has out-degree upper bounded by a function of $\alpha$. They provided an algorithm with $O(\alpha + \log n)$ amortized update time that maintains an orientation with maximum out-degree $O(\alpha)$. In the decades since, this algorithm has found widespread applications in dynamic graph algorithms. Nevertheless, it has remained a stubborn open question whether, when $\alpha = o(\log n)$, the $O(\log n)$ upper bound can be improved. We answer this 27-year-old question in the affirmative, showing that Brodal and Fagerberg's algorithm for maintaining an out-degree $O(\alpha)$ orientation runs in $O(\alpha \cdot \log \log n)$ amortized update time, which is an exponentially-improved dependence on $n$. This is the first improvement on Brodal and Fagerberg's upper bound even for the $\alpha=1$ case of dynamic forests. Our crucial technical innovation is to construct a hierarchy of dynamic graphs with a property we call near isolation. We believe that this construction may be useful for related problems.
item.dc:creator: Sam Hiken, Nicole Wein

item.title: A Note on the Hardness of Partially Dynamic Max Flow
item.description: arXiv:2611.10181v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the fine-grained complexity of partially dynamic max flow in capacitated graphs. Assuming the combinatorial 4-clique hypothesis, combinatorial algorithms require $\Omega(n^{2-o(1)})$ amortized update time. Thus, recomputing max flow after each update is optimal up to subpolynomial factors for combinatorial algorithms in dense graphs. The previous conditional lower bound was $\Omega(n^{1-o(1)})$ amortized update time under SETH or the OMv hypothesis and applies to all algorithms [Dah16].
item.dc:creator: Thatchaphol Saranurak, Benyu Wang

item.title: Fully Dynamic Correlation Clustering with Vertex Updates in Polylogarithmic Update Time
item.description: arXiv:2611.10184v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present a fully dynamic algorithm for correlation clustering that supports \emph{vertex} insertions and deletions while maintaining an $O(1)$ approximation in polylogarithmic amortized update time. This resolves an open problem of vertex deletions posed by a recent line of work on dynamic correlation clustering. We adopt the min-disagreement objective for correlation clustering, i.e., given a signed complete graph $G=(V,E^+\cup E^-)$, we want to minimize the total number of $(+)$ edge crossing clusters and $(-)$ edges within clusters. The input is given in the adjacency list model, where each update inserts or deletes a node along with its full set of $(+)$ neighbors. Our main technical contribution is a fault-tolerant sparse-dense decomposition framework which unlike the existing decomposition-based frameworks allows for structural inconsistencies as long as the induced cost is bounded. We also show a separation between explicitly maintaining the (stronger) sparse-dense decomposition and maintaining a constant-factor approximation to correlation clustering, which may be of independent interest.
item.dc:creator: Vladimir Braverman, Prathamesh Dharangutte, Chenglin Fan, Chen Wang, Shenghao Xie, Samson Zhou

item.title: Flexible Edge Cover: A Disjunctive Programming driven Approximation
item.description: arXiv:2611.10189v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce the flexible edge cover problem, denoted FLEX-EDGE-COVER: the input here is an undirected graph with non-negative edge costs along with a partition of the edges into safe and unsafe edges, non-negative integers $p$ and $q$, and the goal is to find a minimum cost subset of edges such that each vertex has either at least $p$ safe edges incident to it or at least $p+q$ total edges incident to it. We show that FLEX-EDGE-COVER is APX-hard in simple bipartite graphs. A greedy approach leads to a $2$-approximation in all graphs. We show that the $2$-factor can be improved in simple graphs via a novel disjunctive programming-based LP formulation. AI-tools were used in the analysis of our rounding algorithm. Our motivation for introducing and investigating FLEX-EDGE-COVER is its close connection to the Flexible Graph Connectivity problem (denoted $(p,q)$-FGC) which has garnered much recent attention. For $(p,q)$-FGC, we develop a tighter LP-formulation via the disjunctive programming approach. We hope that our disjunctive-programming based LP and rounding algorithms for FLEX-EDGE-COVER will serve as a starting point towards a constant factor approximation for $(p,q)$-FGC.
item.dc:creator: Karthekeyan Chandrasekaran, Krishna Kalathur

item.title: Strong Connectivity Oracle for Multiple Failures via Rooted Flow-Augmentation
item.description: arXiv:2611.10191v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present a significantly improved $k$-fault-tolerant strong connectivity oracle, one of the most basic data structures on a directed graph $G$ that, given any set $F$ of failed edges of size $|F|\le k$, answers whether $G \setminus F$ is strongly connected. For every constant $k$, our oracle only uses $n^{1+o(1)}$ space and $n^{o(1)}$ query time. No prior result can achieve $o(n^{2})$ space and $o(n)$ query time, \emph{even when $k=2$}. Previous oracles either require $\Omega(n)$ query time [BCR18], or $\Omega(n^2)$ space [vdBS19]. Our main technical contribution is a \emph{rooted} version of the highly successful flow augmentation technique, which may be of independent interest. Given a directed graph $G$, an integer $k$, and a source vertex $s$, we can sample a set of edges $A$ such that each minimal $s$-rooted cut of size at most $k$ becomes an $s$-rooted min-cut in $G + A$ with probability $2^{-poly(k)}n^{-o(1)}$.
item.dc:creator: Aditya Anand, Thatchaphol Saranurak, Benyu Wang

item.title: Randomized Greedy MIS Is Fast at Every Node of a Tree
item.description: arXiv:2611.10215v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Randomized Greedy MIS (RGMIS) algorithm computes a maximal independent set (MIS) by processing the vertices in a uniformly random order and greedily adding each vertex to the independent set whenever possible. Despite its simplicity, this algorithm has proved effective in a range of parallel, distributed, and dynamic settings. For sufficiently small maximum degree, Nguyen and Onak (FOCS~'08) and Yoshida, Yamamoto, and Ito (STOC~'09) showed that a recursive simulation of RGMIS can be used to estimate the sizes of matching and vertex cover in sublinear time. The key subroutine in their approach is the following local query procedure: given a vertex $v$, to determine whether $v$ belongs to the MIS, recursively evaluate the neighbors of $v$ that precede $v$ in the random order. If any such neighbor is found to belong to the MIS, the procedure immediately concludes that $v$ is not in the MIS; otherwise, it concludes that $v$ is in the MIS. For graphs of maximum degree $\Delta$, Nguyen and Onak showed that, in expectation over the random ordering, this procedure makes $O(\exp(\Delta))$ recursive calls from a worst-case starting vertex. No better upper bound is known even for trees. We prove that on trees, from \textit{any} starting vertex, this recursive RGMIS procedure makes $\mathrm{poly}(\Delta)$ recursive calls in expectation.
item.dc:creator: Mina Dalirrooyfard, Konstantin Makarychev, Slobodan Mitrovi\'c, Srikkanth Ramachandran

item.title: Lower Bounds Above $\sqrt{3}$ for Online Makespan Minimization on Four Identical Machines
item.description: arXiv:2611.10440v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: For deterministic online makespan minimization, $m = 4$ identical machines is the smallest case whose optimal competitive ratio is open: it is known only to lie between $\sqrt{3} \approx 1.73205$ and $26/15 \approx 1.73333$. We prove a lower bound of $14383/8304 \approx 1.73206$ using a single branching layer, and refine the construction with a second, mirrored branching layer to obtain $14350/8283 \approx 1.73246$, closing about a third of the gap. Our constructions are the first branching adversaries for $m = 4$ machines, and the first explicit lower bounds for online makespan minimization in which the adversary presents jobs in non-monotone order of size.
item.dc:creator: Maximilian Janke

item.title: Close and Sort: Exact Maximum-Likelihood Aggregation of Cyclic Rank-Two Preferences
item.description: arXiv:2611.10538v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Pairwise probabilities arise in rank aggregation, recommendation, and human or LLM evaluation, yet converting them into a maximum-likelihood list is a weighted Kemeny problem and is NP-hard in general. Known exact algorithms for rank-two tournaments use only comparison signs and do not optimize this likelihood. We show that the weighted problem is exactly solvable when the skew-symmetric log-odds matrix $W_{ij}=\log(p_{ij}/p_{ji})$ has rank two, including when the induced preferences contain cycles. Writing $W_{ij}=\det(h_i,h_j)$ and adding the closing vector $h_0=-\sum_i h_i$ turns the objective into twice the signed area of a closed polygon. This geometry yields CloseSort, which polar-sorts the $n+1$ edge vectors, cuts after $h_0$, and returns a global maximum-likelihood order in $O(n\log n)$ time from the factors. The same geometry identifies the runner-up and gives a stability certificate beyond exact rank two. When the smallest determinant $\delta$ of two consecutive edges in the closed angular cycle is positive, it is exactly the best-to-runner-up log-likelihood gap. For $W=W_0+E$, the CloseSort order of $W_0$ has regret at most $\sum_{i<j}|E_{ij}|$ on $W$ and remains optimal whenever this sum is below $\delta$, a worst-case tight threshold. In 5,120 determinant-logit simulations, increasing the observations per pair from 4 to 64 raises the fraction on which rank-two projection outperforms the empirical plug-in optimum from 68.6% to 85.7%. On 3,600 Arena-Hard LLM-judge profiles drawn from 63 systems and ten judges, the leading rank-two component captures 89.2% of the log-odds energy. On profiles containing a directed majority triangle, CloseSort reduces normalized regret by 44% relative to Borda and improves the mean normalized objective over each of eight baselines. With factors supplied, it is 8,407 times faster than exact dynamic programming on 18-item rankings.
item.dc:creator: Kehan Liu, Zhaoyun Chen, Xianquan Yan

item.title: An Improved Algorithm for Quantified Boolean Formulas
item.description: arXiv:2611.10633v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantified Boolean formula (QBF), the quantified version of Boolean satisfiability (SAT), is a fundamental problem in constraint solving. Due to the $\mathsf{PSPACE}$-complete nature of QBF, designing theoretically efficient QBF algorithms is much harder and receives less attention in academia. In this work, we present a new algorithm based on memoized search, which solves QBF with $n$ variables and $m$ clauses in $1.685^m\cdot\text{poly}(n)$ time and space. This is the first improvement over the $1.709^m\cdot\text{poly}(n)$ bound by Williams in over 20 years. Our technique is based on the minimum vertex cover of the conflict graphs, which was proposed to study the parameterized complexity of SAT. We extend this idea to QBF and further show that QBF is slicewise polynomial-time solvable using this parameter.
item.dc:creator: Zhiyang Chen, Hailong Yao

item.title: Tunnels: Compressing the Solution Subgraph of Regular Path Queries
item.description: arXiv:2611.10736v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Regular path queries (RPQs) are increasingly expected to return the paths that match them, not only their endpoints. Since the number of matching paths can be exponential or infinite, a standard way to deliver them (PMR) is the subgraph $\Hs$ of the product between the graph and the query automaton that contains exactly the nodes lying on some solution path. We show that $\Hs$ can be compressed much further when the graph is available to the decoder: most of $\Hs$ can be regenerated by re-running small parts of the traversal, and only the places where the traversal would waste significant effort on dead branches need to be stored. We formalize this as \emph{tunnels}: regions of $\Hs$ that are re-expanded from a stored entry point with a bounded amount of extra work, either an absolute budget or one proportional to the output produced. We handle the three classes of RPQs: constant-to-variable, constant-to-constant, and variable-to-variable. In the latter, we study the combination of tunnels with cutting the query at a selective articulation point of the automaton and encoding the answer as a union of Cartesian products of leftward and rightward traversals. Our experimental results show improvements of 2 to 3 orders of magnitude over the baseline space of PMR, for an acceptable increase in traversal time.
item.dc:creator: Adri\'an G\'omez-Brand\'on, Gonzalo Navarro

item.title: Solving Large Rubik's Cubes within a Factor of $2.37+o(1)$ of Optimal
item.description: arXiv:2611.11018v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We design optimized algorithms to solve the $n \times n \times n$ Rubik's Cube within $30.5 n^2 / \lg n + o(n^2 / \lg n)$ moves. This upper bound is asymptotically within a factor of $2.37$ of the known lower bound, which applies to almost all instances. The constant $30.5$ is also the first explicit constant factor for the known upper bound of $O(n^2 / \lg n)$, where the implicit constant of the previous algorithm was $1.01 \cdot 10^{40}$ (ten duodecillion). Thus we improve the upper-bound constant by a factor of more than $3.30 \cdot 10^{38}$ (330 undecillion). Our algorithm runs in time linear in the input size $N = \Theta(n^2)$, and uses $O(\sqrt{N} \lg N)$ extra space (beyond the state of the cube). Our implementation is the first practical cube solver to generate solutions of length $O(n^2/\lg n)$. Our latest solver outperforms existing solvers for $n$ as small as $840$.
item.dc:creator: Jeremy Mrzyglocki, Tomas Rokicki, Maxine Perroni-Scharf, Erik D. Demaine

item.title: Optimal Polynomial-Query Approximation for Consistent Submodular Maximization with Short Lookahead
item.description: arXiv:2611.11124v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Elements arrive one at a time, and after each arrival an algorithm holds a set of at most $k$ arrived elements. Its goal is a held set whose value under a monotone submodular function is close to the best value that $k$ arrived elements can achieve. The recourse of an update is the number of elements inserted into or removed from the held set, and we require it to be bounded independently of $k$ and of the number $n$ of arrivals. With evaluations only on sets of arrived elements and polynomially many of them, the best ratio a randomized algorithm can achieve is $2-\sqrt{2}\approx0.5858$. We show that seeing future arrivals raises the best ratio for polynomially many evaluations to $1-1/e\approx0.6321$, for deterministic and for randomized algorithms; no algorithm with polynomially many evaluations exceeds $1-1/e$, even when all elements are available at once. For every $\varepsilon>0$, a deterministic algorithm that sees the next $\lceil\varepsilon k/3\rceil$ arrivals keeps a set of value at least $1-1/e-\varepsilon$ times the optimum at every time, changes $O(\varepsilon^{-3})$ elements per arrival and makes $(n+1)^{O(\varepsilon^{-2})}$ evaluations. With the whole arrival sequence known in advance, a deterministic algorithm attains the same ratio with $O(\varepsilon^{-2})$ changes per arrival. A randomized algorithm with the same short lookahead makes $O(n^2k)$ evaluations, changes $O(\varepsilon^{-2})$ elements per arrival, and attains the same ratio in expectation at each fixed time. The main tool is a greedy algorithm with an explicit guarantee for each of its partial solutions combined with each initial segment of the known future arrivals. A second tool moves between two such solutions one element at a time while keeping the value high, and the deterministic algorithm times each move using upper bounds on the optimum from failed searches.
item.dc:creator: Vaneet Aggarwal

item.title: Online Correlated Exponential Clocks
item.description: arXiv:2611.11133v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In online resource allocation, we seek to allocate an incoming sequence of requests $j \in J$ among a set of offline resources $i \in I$, where decisions must be made immediately without knowledge of the future. State-of-the-art results typically follow from relax-and-round methods. For many problems, recent advances have come from improved methods of online rounding with negative correlations. However, such rounding schemes have largely been implemented on a case-by-case basis, making it difficult to transfer improvements and new ideas between problem settings. This leads us to ask the question: Can we develop unified methods of online rounding with negative correlations which can obtain state-of-the-art guarantees across different resource allocation settings? We answer this question affirmatively by introducing the framework of Online Correlated Exponential Clocks (OCEC). In this framework, fractional allocations $x_{ij}$ are assigned exponential clocks $Y_{ij} \sim \mathrm{Exp}(x_{ij})$, and each request $j$ is allocated to the resource $i$ with smallest $Y_{ij}$. The key idea is that the sequence $(Y_{ij})_j$ for each fixed $i$ is negatively correlated via an OCEC generator, resulting in better-than-baseline guarantees. Our contributions are two-fold: First, we introduce OCEC rounding as a problem-independent interface which any online algorithm can use. This isolates the challenge of online rounding into the self-contained problem of designing an effective OCEC generator. Second, we demonstrate the flexibility of this method by giving a single OCEC generator which yields improved competitive bounds in three distinct problems: 0.556 for Display Ads, 0.530 for AdWords, and 4.69 for squared-load balancing. Previous best results were obtained by Blanc and Charikar (FOCS 2021), Chen, Huang, and Sun (FOCS 2024), and Borst and Kashaev (SODA 2027), respectively.
item.dc:creator: Zhiyi Huang, Kalen Patton, Peilin Yang, Jiahao Zhao

item.title: Fast Approximate $\ell_p$ Chamfer Distance via Lopsided Embeddings and Structured JL
item.description: arXiv:2611.11151v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: For two $d$-dimensional point sets $A, B$ of size $n$, the Chamfer distance from $A$ to $B$ is defined as $\text{CH}(A,B)=\sum_{a \in A} \min_{b \in B} \mathsf{dist}(a, b)$, where $\mathsf{dist}$ is some underlying distance measure. We present efficient algorithms for approximating the Chamfer distance under the $\ell_p$ norm for $1 < p \le 2$. For the general case $1 < p < 2$, we utilize lopsided $\ell_p$ to $\ell_1$ embeddings with weak guarantees. We show that they are sufficient for preserving the Chamfer distance. In the high-dimensional regime, we use Fast Matrix Multiplication techniques to speed up the lopsided embeddings. These lead to $O(nd\cdot \mathrm{poly}(\log \log n, \log(1/\varepsilon))/\varepsilon^2)$ total time. For the specific Euclidean case ($p=2$), we leverage the Fast Johnson-Lindenstrauss Transform based on Toeplitz matrices and re-analyze the previous $\ell_1$-specific Chamfer algorithm in $\ell_2$. These achieve a runtime matching the recent state-of-the-art $\ell_1$ result of $O(nd(\log \log n + \log (1/\varepsilon))/\varepsilon^2)$, improving upon the previous $O(nd \log n/\varepsilon^2)$ bound for $\ell_2$. We also give additional results for the angular distance and upper and lower bounds in the streaming setting.
item.dc:creator: Ying Feng, David P. Woodruff

item.title: Algorithms for Soft Tree Containment on Tree-Child Networks
item.description: arXiv:2611.11236v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Phylogenetic networks generalize evolutionary trees by allowing lineages to merge. The Tree Containment problem asks whether a network $N$ displays a tree $T$ on the same taxa. When the polytomies of $T$ reflect uncertainty rather than simultaneous divergence, the relevant notion is soft display, in which $N$ may refine the polytomies of $T$. We take it in its asymmetric reading. Soft Tree Containment is NP-hard on reticulation-visible networks even at reticulation indegree three, and it was open for a non-binary tree and a tree-child network with multifurcating tree nodes or reticulations of indegree above two. We solve this case. A cluster characterization reduces soft display to realizing all clusters of $T$ by one switching, and in a tree-child network the vertices that can realize a cluster lie on a single chain. The per-cluster requirements then form a constraint network of width one, which arc consistency decides without search, and a $2$-SAT instance when $N$ is binary. This yields, to our knowledge, the first polynomial-time algorithm for soft Tree Containment on single-labelled tree-child networks of arbitrary reticulation indegree, and a linear-time algorithm when $T$ is binary. The same method decides the symmetric variant of the problem, in which the polytomies of $N$ may be resolved as well.
item.dc:creator: Erdem Ugurlu, Louxin Zhang

item.title: Linear Set Reconciliation with $O(d)$ Additive Redundancy
item.description: arXiv:2611.11409v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In set reconciliation, two parties holding sets $A, B \subseteq [n]$ with $|A \triangle B| \le d$ seek to recover their symmetric difference from short $\mathbb{F}_2$-linear sketches, which is equivalent to recovering a $d$-sparse vector $x = \mathbf{1}_{A \triangle B} \in \mathbb{F}_2^n$ from its syndrome $Hx \in \mathbb{F}_2^m$. While the information-theoretic counting bound requires $L(n,d) := \log \sum_{i=0}^d \binom{n}{i} = d\log(n/d) + \Theta(d)$ bits, existing polynomial-time schemes either use at least $d\lceil\log(n+1)\rceil$ bits (algebraic sketches, leaving an $\Omega(d\log d)$-bit gap) or incur a multiplicative $(1+\delta)L(n,d)$ overhead (peeling-based sketches), raising the question of whether $L(n,d) + O(d)$ bits is achievable with fast updates and decoding. We construct a public-coin randomized $\mathbb{F}_2$-linear sketch of length $L(n,d) + O(d) + \lambda\log^{O(1)} n$ that recovers each fixed input of weight at most $d$ with probability at least $1 - 2^{-\lambda}$, with $\log^{O(1)} n$ update time and $d\exp(O((\log\log n)^2)) = dn^{o(1)}$ worst-case decoding time. In particular, for $n \le 2^{\operatorname{polylog}(d)}$ and $\lambda \le d^{1-\Omega(1)}$, this achieves $L(n,d) + O(d)$ bits with $\operatorname{polylog}(d)$ update time and $d^{1+o(1)}$ decoding time. Our construction encodes $d$ permuted rows via randomly scaled Pinsketch syndromes and sketches the resulting bit array column by column. Decoding columns sequentially from prefix predictions cancels recovered rows and exposes undecided rows as decoder-side hints, reducing each column to a hinted sparse recovery problem that we solve via a recursive sketch, HintSketch.
item.dc:creator: Tianren Liu, Rui Xu, Tong Yang, Kangyang Zhou

item.title: Tight B-Trees for Adjacency Labeling
item.description: arXiv:2611.11444v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We show that planar graphs admit adjacency labels of size $\log n+O(\log\log n)$: every vertex gets a label of this many bits, and the adjacency of two vertices is decided from their labels alone, in constant time. This improves the $\log n+O(\sqrt{\log n\log\log n})$ of Dujmovi\'c et al. (J. ACM 2021) and the $\log n+O(\sqrt{\log n})$ of Gawrychowski and Janczewski (SOSA 2022). Equivalently, $n$-vertex planar graphs have an induced-universal graph with $n(\log n)^{O(1)}$ vertices, down from $n2^{O(\sqrt{\log n})}$. The same holds for graphs of bounded genus, apex-minor-free graphs and $k$-planar graphs. For every proper minor-closed class we get $\log n+O(\sqrt{\log n\log\log n})$, down from the $\log n+O((\log n)^{3/4})$ of Dujmovi\'c et al. (2026). Both results come from tight B-trees: nodes are split into parts of nearly equal size, so every node but the topmost stays within a factor $1\pm O(1/\log n)$ of its target size, and a root-to-leaf path loses only $O(\log\log n)$ bits.
item.dc:creator: Noy Rotbart

item.title: \~Optimal Facial Distance Labeling in Planar Graph
item.description: arXiv:2611.11479v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We show how to assign labels of size $\tilde O(n^{1/3})$ to the vertices of a face $F$ in an $n$-vertex unweighted undirected planar graph $G$ s.t one can deduce the distance between any two vertices of $F$ given their labels alone. This matches (up to log factors) the $\Omega(n^{1/3})$ lower bound of Gavoille, Peleg, P\'erennes, Raz from 2004. Prior to our work, the smallest labels were of size $O(n^{1/2})$.
item.dc:creator: Noy Rotbart, Oren Weimann

item.title: Amortized Cell-Probe Lower Bounds for Dynamic Boolean Problems
item.description: arXiv:2611.11508v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We prove the first unconditional amortized $\Omega\big((\log N/\log\log N)^2\big)$ cell-probe lower bound for a Boolean dynamic problem. For insert-only multiphase Disjointness with $N$ query sets over $[N]$ and word size $w=\Theta(\log N)$, a fixed distribution of interleaved insertions and queries forces this expected average cost per operation, excluding preprocessing. The bound allows sufficiently small constant error for each query of every fixed legal sequence and imposes no restriction on individual operation costs. It transfers to incremental directed reachability, incremental subgraph connectivity, and fully dynamic triangle detection. We also prove $t_q=\Omega\big((\log N/\log(t_uw))^2\big)$ for amortized insertion time $1\le t_u=N^{o(1)}$ and expected query time $t_q$, when the number of insertions before the final query is not announced in advance. We reach the quadratic-logarithmic scale with bounded error by combining interleaving with the 2.5-round communication framework [Ko26a, Ko26b] and controlling errors among accepted simulations.
item.dc:creator: Young Kun Ko

item.title: Induced-Minor-Free Graphs Admit a Star-Based Separator of Size $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{n})$
item.description: arXiv:2611.11513v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Given an $H$-induced-minor-free graph $G$ with $n$ vertices, we construct a balanced separator of $G$ consisting of $\tilde{O}(|V(H)|\sqrt{n})$ star subgraphs. Our result is an induced-minor-free analog of the famous separator theorem for $H$-minor-free graphs by Alon, Seymour, and Thomas [J. Amer. Math. Soc., 1990]. A key idea in our construction is a new decomposition of $H$-induced-minor-free graphs, analogous to the cop decomposition for $H$-minor-free graphs by Andreae [J. Combin. Theory Ser. B, 1986]. We also discuss several algorithmic applications of our result.
item.dc:creator: Arnold Filtser, Nikolai Karol, Hung Le, Florian Lehner

item.title: Internal Queries for Maximal Closed Substrings
item.description: arXiv:2611.11552v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Searching for repetitions inside a selected part of a text raises a subtle boundary problem: removing neighbouring characters can create new maximal answers. We study this effect for maximal closed substrings (MCSs). A string is closed if it is a single letter or has a nonempty proper prefix occurring exactly twice, as its prefix and suffix; a closed occurrence is maximal if neither available one-character extension is closed. Previous work established $O(n\log n)$ bounds on the global MCS families of a length-$n$ text and developed enumeration algorithms. Internal queries instead ask for the MCSs of a chosen substring, with maximality evaluated inside that substring. Separating boundary occurrences from interior ones gives an $O(n\log n)$-word index that reports the $c$ answers in $O(\log n+c)$ time and supports counting and longest queries in $O(\log n)$ time. Our main result reduces reporting space to $O(n)$ words, with $O((c+1)\log^{1+\varepsilon} n)$ query time and $O(n\log^{1+\varepsilon} n)$ construction time for any fixed $\varepsilon>0$. Thus, after preprocessing, reporting requires no additive scan of the queried substring, which is particularly useful for long queries with few answers. Independently, we prove that at most $3(s-1)$ MCS occurrences of any length-$s$ substring cross a fixed gap between consecutive characters, with maximality evaluated inside that substring. The same bound holds for global MCSs contained in a length-$s$ block. A family over two letters attains $\lfloor(s-1)/2\rfloor$ crossings for every $s\ge3$, showing that the linear order of this local density bound is optimal.
item.dc:creator: Simone Faro, Francesco Pio Marino, Arianna Pavone

item.title: How Far Must a Test Explore? Certifying Composable Read-Write Interfaces from Their Own Random Edits
item.description: arXiv:2611.11899v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Random tests of stateful code check laws, like reading back a written value, at states that random writes reach. The laws hold at every state exactly when the code behaves like a record with hidden data, so a pass is taken as evidence. This can fail: the laws can hold at every sample while the code is far from any record. The laws are local, but behaving like a record is global. Self-testing and stability theorems bridge this gap when the query distribution is controlled by the tester or preserved by the tested maps, but here it is generated by the tested writes, which need not be invertible. We ask how far a test must explore. An interface has $m$ binary variables, each with a read and two writes; in a record, reads return their bits and writes set only their bits. Samples are the ends of geometric runs of mean $\ell$ of uniformly random writes from a start distribution; a tester adds its own write chains of depth $d$. The distance is the least, over records with hidden data, of the largest probability that a read or write differs from it at a sample. From one start state, law checks at $O(m^2\log m/\epsilon)$ samples certify, at fixed confidence, any threshold $\epsilon$ after geometric runs of every positive mean, while runs of fixed positive length can pass at distance $1/2$. For the worst start distribution, take $\epsilon=m^{-\beta}$ with fixed $0<\beta\le1$. For $d\le cm$ with fixed $c<1/2$, a polynomial budget of samples and writes exists exactly when $\ell=\Omega(m)$, where law checks suffice. With no runs, the least depth for this budget is $(1/2+o(1))m$. Counting samples alone, in the worst case at $\epsilon=1/(32m)$ and $d\le m/16$, the critical mean for a polynomial budget is $\Theta(m\log(m/d)/\log m)$, by exhaustive search. So one start state needs only law checks, and the worst case at these thresholds needs exploration linear in $m$ if writes are counted.
item.dc:creator: Jiaxuan Guo, Xingyu Ren, Jingxin Yang, Youran Sun, Haizhao Yang

item.title: Tight Bounds for Sublinear Metric Steiner Tree
item.description: arXiv:2611.11986v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In the metric Steiner tree problem we are given an $n$-point metric space $(V,w)$ and a set $T\subseteq V$ of terminals, and we seek the smallest weight $\mathrm{OPT}$ of a tree that spans $T$ and may use points of $V\setminus T$. We study sublinear algorithms in the distance-oracle model, where the algorithm knows $V$ and $T$ upfront and can query the distance function $w$. The objective is to estimate $\mathrm{OPT}$ while querying significantly fewer than $n^2$ distances. The minimum spanning tree on $T$ estimates $\mathrm{OPT}$ within a factor $2$, and its weight can be approximated with $\widetilde{O}(n)$ queries. The natural question that has been studied is therefore the query complexity of estimating $\mathrm{OPT}$ within a factor strictly below $2$. Chen, Khanna, and Tan [SODA 2023] gave such an algorithm using $\widetilde{O}(n^{13/7})$ queries, and a lower bound of $\widetilde\Omega(n^{6/5})$. Later Mahabadi, Roghani, Tarnawski, and Vakilian [ITCS 2025] improved the algorithm to $\widetilde{O}(n^{5/3})$, and Mahabadi, Tarnawski, and Vakilian [ITCS 2027] improved the lower bound to $\widetilde{\Omega}(n^{7/5})$. In this work we settle the above question. We give an algorithm that estimates $\mathrm{OPT}$ within a factor $2-\eta_0$, for an absolute constant $\eta_0>0$, with query (and time) complexity $\widetilde{O}(n^{3/2})$. We also show that the exponent $3/2$ is tight.
item.dc:creator: Sepideh Mahabadi, Mohammad Roghani, Jakub Tarnawski, Ali Vakilian

item.title: The Power of Migration on Identical Machines is Two
item.description: arXiv:2611.12034v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the power of migration in preemptive scheduling on identical parallel machines with time windows. If an instance admits a migratory schedule on $m$ machines, how many machines are needed to schedule it without migration? Kalyanasundaram and Pruhs (2001) showed that $6m-5$ machines suffice and gave a polynomial-time construction using $12m-5$ machines, whereas $2m-1$ machines may be necessary. We close this gap, which has been open for more than 25 years: $2m-1$ machines always suffice, and a corresponding non-migratory schedule can be computed in strongly polynomial time. Our proof has two main technical ingredients. First, we introduce supercanonical schedules and prove that the conflict graph of every such schedule on $m$ machines is $(2m-1)$-colorable. The key property is that whenever a job pauses, the jobs running alongside it just before and just after the pause separate the jobs processed entirely during the pause from the rest of the conflict graph. We use these separators and Kempe exchanges to compute a coloring in polynomial time. Second, we construct a supercanonical schedule with polynomially many processing blocks by shrinking job windows as far as possible while preserving feasibility and solving a min-cost flow problem.
item.dc:creator: Nicole Megow, Bart Zondervan

item.title: Longest Unbordered Factors in Linear Time
item.description: arXiv:2611.12146v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A border of a string is a nonempty proper prefix that is also a suffix. A string is unbordered if it has no border. The length of a longest unbordered factor is closely related to the smallest period of the string. While the smallest period can be computed in linear time, the best previously known algorithm for computing a longest unbordered factor takes $O(n \log n)$ worst-case time for a string of length $n$. Whether this computational problem can be solved in worst-case linear time has remained open. In this paper, we resolve this open problem for integer alphabets of size $n^{O(1)}$ by presenting an algorithm that computes all occurrences of longest unbordered factors in $O(n)$ worst-case time. Our algorithm uses a combinatorial property of longest unbordered factors and scans the input string in both directions to capture all occurrences achieving the global maximum without computing the local maximum at every starting position.
item.dc:creator: Takuya Mieno

item.title: Instance-Optimality of Single-Pair Personalized PageRank
item.description: arXiv:2611.12198v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We consider discounted random walks in a directed simple graph $G=(V,E)$. Such a walk terminates at each step with a constant probability $\alpha\in (0,1)$ and otherwise continues to a uniform random out-neighbor. Given a pair $(s,t)\in V^2$, we denote by $\pi(s,t)$ the probability of such a discounted random walk starting at $s$ terminates at $t$. This probability is referred to as the Personalized PageRank (PPR) of $t$ with respect to $s$. The problem of estimating $\pi(s,t)$ within a constant multiplicative factor with constant success probability for a given vertex pair $(s,t)$ is called the single-pair PPR estimation problem. We investigate the instance-optimality of single-pair PPR estimation in directed graphs. We present a new algorithm that aims at instance-optimal running time up to polylogarithmic factors. In other words, no correct algorithm can run faster than our algorithm on any valid graph by more than a polylogarithmic factor. We show that our algorithm is instance-optimal in the standard adjacency-list query model if $n$ is not known (as is often the case for most of the large networks to which PPR is applied). When $n$ is known, our algorithm is still instance-optimal for sparse graphs. For denser graphs, when $n$ is known, we show that no algorithm can achieve general instance-optimality. For the multiplicative approximation of PPR, we also improve the worst-case complexity from $O(mn\log n)$ to the near-optimal $O(m\log n)$. This is not only for the single-pair discussed above, but also for the single-source and single-target variants of the PPR estimation problem.
item.dc:creator: Christian Bertram, Mads Vestergaard Jensen, Mikkel Thorup, Hanzhi Wang, Shuyi Yan

item.title: Tight Competitive Bounds for Online Matching on Forests
item.description: arXiv:2611.12210v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the online matching problem, its fractional relaxation, and the fractional online vertex cover problem on forests whose edges arrive one at a time in an arbitrary order. Matching decisions are irrevocable, and vertex-cover weights can only increase over time. For online matching, we present a randomized algorithm with expected competitive ratio $4/7$ against an oblivious adversary, improving the previous $5/9$ guarantee. We also present a deterministic algorithm that simultaneously maintains a $4/7$-competitive fractional matching and a $7/4$-competitive fractional vertex cover. This deterministic algorithm improves the previous $5/9$ guarantee for fractional matching and the $11/6$ guarantee for fractional vertex cover. We prove that $4/7$ is optimal for both randomized and fractional matching, even on growing trees of maximum degree four.
item.dc:creator: Bart{\l}omiej Bosek, Grzegorz Gutowski, Pawe{\l} Putra, Anna Zych-Pawlewicz

item.title: A 1.764-competitive algorithm for online fractional vertex cover on forests
item.description: arXiv:2611.12237v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study online fractional vertex cover on forests under edge arrival. We give a deterministic algorithm with competitive ratio at most $4 - \sqrt{5} \approx 1.764$, which simultaneously produces an online fractional matching with competitive ratio of at least $1/(4 - \sqrt{5}) \approx 0.566$. This improves on the previous best competitive ratios of $11/6 \approx 1.833$ and $5/9 \approx 0.555$, respectively.
item.dc:creator: Marcin Bienkowski

item.title: Strong Backdoor to Forests is FPT: Tight Linear-Time FPT for Essentially General SAT
item.description: arXiv:2611.12321v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In a seminal work, Gaspers and Szeider [FOCS 2013] gave a fixed-parameter tractable (FPT) approximate algorithm for finding a strong backdoor of size at most $k$ to incidence treewidth at most $t$, for a given CNF-formula $\phi$. In particular, their algorithm runs in $f(k,t) |\phi|^3$ time, and finds a strong backdoor to treewidth at most $t$, of $\phi$, of size at most $2^k$ whenever there exists one of size at most $k$. Determining whether the detection of strong backdoors to bounded incidence treewidth is FPT parameterized by $k+t$ was left open in their work and this has been repeatedly posed as an open question by Gaspers and Szeider, for example in [The Multivariate Algorithmic Revolution and Beyond 2012] and more recently in [Computer Science Reviews 2025], even for incidence forests and when the input is a $3$-CNF formula. We answer this question affirmatively. We show that strong backdoors to forests can be found in linear-FPT time on arbitrary non-tautological CNF formulas (not just on 3-CNF formulas). Given such a formula $\phi$ and a budget $k$, our algorithm finds a strong backdoor to the class of forests, of size at most $k$, or correctly reports that none exists, in $2^{2^{O(k)}} |\phi|$ time. Moreover, we show that our result is as tight as it can get. First, we show that finding strong backdoors to treewidth $t$ for any $t \geq 2$ is W[1]-hard, even on non-tautological 3-CNF formulas. Second, the running time of our algorithm is tight: it is linear in the input size and a better than double-exponential dependence on $k$ in the running time would imply a $2^{o(N/\log N)}$-time algorithm for solving 3-SAT on $N$ variables, which would beat even the very recently claimed sub-exponential algorithm for solving 3-SAT by OpenAI and Anthropic.
item.dc:creator: Olesia Bilyk, Aidar Munduzbaev, Roohani Sharma, Mamnoon Siam

item.title: How Hard Is Tokenisation? Algorithms and Complexity Beyond NP-Hardness
item.description: arXiv:2611.12348v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Given a collection of strings and a vocabulary budget, how well can we minimize its total token count, and how does the answer change with the tokenisation model? For binary direct tokenisation, previous work proved APX-hardness but left constant-factor approximability unresolved \citep{kastreva2026}. We rule out every polynomial-time $M^{1-\varepsilon}$ approximation, for fixed $\varepsilon>0$, unless $\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}$, even on distinct equal-length strings with $K=m-1$. Here $M$ is the total input length and $m$ is the number of input strings. We complement this lower bound with a deterministic polynomial-time $O(M/\log M)$ approximation algorithm and stronger bounds for selected vocabulary budgets. For the different objective of maximizing compression savings, GreedTok was shown to attain a constant fraction of the optimum on unrestricted alphabets \citep{baliga2026}; we establish a deterministic EPTAS for direct savings on every fixed alphabet and analyze greedy selection by true marginal gains. For exact optimization, we give a binary direct algorithm running in $2^{O(n\log\log n/\log n)}\poly(I)$ time, where $n$ is the total length of the distinct input strings and $I$ is the input encoding length. Finally, we resolve two unary merge-model hardness questions left by the bounded-alphabet study \citep{kastreva2026}: standard unary bottom-up tokenisation is APX-hard, and unary optimal pair encoding is strongly NP-complete, strengthening the previously known weak hardness.
item.dc:creator: Andrei Robert Ion, Rares Mateiu, Adrian Miclaus, Alexandru Popa

item.title: Optimizing the Steady-State Travel Time of Nash Flows over Time with Capacity Increases
item.description: arXiv:2611.12486v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study budgeted capacity augmentation for single-source single-sink \NFOTs under constant inflow $u_0$. The goal is to increase capacities on arcs subject to a global budget constraint in order to minimize the steady-state travel time in the network. We show that this problem is weakly NP-hard on series-parallel networks and provide an exact pseudopolynomial algorithm as well as a fully polynomial algorithm that attains the optimum travel time for budget $B$ while spending at most $B + \varepsilon\cdot\max\{B,u_0\}$. On general networks the problem becomes strongly NP-hard. Moreover, unless $\text{P} = \text{NP}$, for every fixed $\varepsilon \in (0,1)$, no polynomial-time algorithm can achieve the optimal steady-state travel time while exceeding the budget by at most a factor of $n^{1-\varepsilon}$. Lastly, we give structural properties about steady-state travel time under varying arc capacities. We identify capacity thresholds determined by subsets of $s$-$t$-cuts and show that the travel time is constant in the interior of the cells resulting from the corresponding hyperplane arrangement.
item.dc:creator: Niklas Dahlmeier, Paul Paschmanns, Laura Ritter, Ruben Skorupinski

item.title: Better Bounds For Graph Reconstruction
item.description: arXiv:2611.12619v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The goal in graph reconstruction problems is to learn an initially unknown graph using only a few queries of a specific type. Possibly the most natural query type is retrieving the distance between any two vertices of a connected, undirected, and unweighted graph. For a bounded-degree graph on $n$ vertices, Kannan, Mathieu, and Zhou [TALG 2018] showed a randomized algorithm that uses only $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(n^{3/2})$ such queries. On the lower bound side, it is only known that any randomized algorithm needs $\Omega(n\log n)$ queries. We make a significant step forward to bridging these bounds by designing a randomized algorithm that uses $n^{4/3+o(1)}$ queries. This requires extending the original approach based on Voronoi diagrams into a recursive procedure that partitions a cell into smaller cells. While such a recursive approach has been used in the related graph verification problem, in the more general graph reconstruction problem we need to operate without knowing the graph, which requires a new (and more technical) approach.
item.dc:creator: Antoni Buraczewski, Pawe{\l} Gawrychowski

item.title: Polynomial-Space Quantum Algorithms from Classical Branching: Colouring, Domination and Monotone Local Search
item.description: arXiv:2611.12714v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We give quantum algorithms for exponential-time problems on $n$ vertices or elements, with bounded error, polynomial space and no quantum random access memory. Our results are these. (1) 4-Colouring in quantum time $O(1.3032^n)$, from a polynomial-space branching algorithm with polynomial-space terminal algorithms; with the branching algorithm alone, $O(1.3100^n)$. The previous best bound in this model, to our knowledge, is $O(1.3231^n)$. (2) $k$-Colouring below the previous best bound for $k \in \{5, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11\}$ and $13 \le k \le 18$, from $O(1.4518^n)$ for $k = 5$ to $O(1.9233^n)$ for $k = 18$. (3) Dominating Set in $O(1.2235^n)$, against the previous $O(2^{n/2})$, Independent Dominating Set in $O(1.1583^n)$, and Edge Dominating Set and Minimum Maximal Matching in $O(1.1501^n)$. (4) A quantum form of monotone local search: if the extension problem has a backtracking tree with $c^k$ nodes up to polynomial factors, the problem is solved in quantum time $(2 - 1/c)^{n/2}$ up to polynomial factors. This gives Feedback Vertex Set in $O(1.3081^n)$, Subset and Group Feedback Vertex Set in $O(1.3229^n)$, Cluster Vertex Deletion in $O(1.2033^n)$, 3-Hitting Set in $O(1.2405^n)$, Proper Interval Vertex Deletion in $O(1.3541^n)$, Multicut on Trees in $O(1.1647^n)$ and Min-Ones $d$-SAT in $O^*((2-1/d)^{n/2})$. (5) Quantum exponential-time approximations below the quantum exact bounds, such as a 1.1-approximation for Vertex Cover in $O(1.0555^n)$ and for Feedback Vertex Set in $O(1.2161^n)$. The colouring exponents for $k \ge 6$ come from an evaluation of a known reduction recursion, computed in floating point with a margin.
item.dc:creator: Sebastian Senge

item.title: Flows in High Degree Places: Sublinear Spanning Tree Congestion
item.description: arXiv:2611.12827v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The congestion of a spanning tree $T$ of graph $G$ is the maximum congestion of an edge of $T$ if each edge of $G$ is routed on $T$. Prior work showed that obtaining a minimum congestion spanning tree is NP-hard to approximate within $6/5$, yet the only known approximation algorithm is a trivial $n/2$-approximation from returning any spanning tree of the graph. We give a simple poly-time $\tilde{O}(n^{6/7})$-approximation for minimum congestion spanning tree on $n$-vertex graphs. We obtain this result via a $\tilde{O}(m^{2/3})$-approximation, where $m$ is the number of edges. Our algorithm is based on a new \textit{flow-or-degree decomposition} which deletes a small number of edges so that each remaining component either has low degree or admits a low congestion flow. We also show that, assuming the Small Set Expansion Hypothesis, it is NP-hard to $O(1)$-approximate this problem, even on graphs of constant maximum degree.
item.dc:creator: D Ellis Hershkowitz, Richard Z Huang

item.title: Optimal Injectivity of the SparseStack
item.description: arXiv:2611.12867v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: An Oblivious Subspace Injection (OSI) is a random sketching matrix that reliably preserves the minimum singular value of any fixed subspace with high constant probability, requiring only a one-sided spectral lower bound without controlling upper singular values. While classical Oblivious Subspace Embeddings (OSEs) fundamentally require row sparsity $\Omega(\log r)$ at linear sketch dimension $k = O(r)$, we show that one-sided injectivity permits strictly sparser sketches, establishing matching (up to $\log\log r$ factors) upper and lower bounds of $\tilde{\Theta}(\sqrt{\log r})$. First, we prove that the SparseStack sketch achieves constant injectivity at linear dimension $k = \Theta(r)$ with row sparsity only $\zeta = O(\sqrt{\log r})$, well below the $\Theta(\log r)$ barrier where standard operator-norm concentration fails. Second, we establish a matching lower bound: any isotropic random sketching matrix satisfying a mild row-overlap condition requires row sparsity $\zeta = \Omega(\sqrt{\log r / \log \log r})$ to achieve linear-dimension injectivity, confirming that the $\sqrt{\log r}$ scale is fundamental. To bypass the lack of an operator-norm upper bound when $\zeta = O(\sqrt{\log r})$, we decouple the sketch into two independent halves and introduce three techniques: (i) a uniform lower bound for flat vectors via randomized rounding, controlling discretization error using solely the Frobenius norm; (ii) a Gaussian truncation and minimax duality argument showing that all non-flat vectors escaping injectivity in the first half concentrate on a single universal coordinate subset $I \subseteq [n]$ of size $O(r/\zeta)$, bypassing union bounds over supports; and (iii) a two-tier coordinate isolation analysis in the second half that suppresses collisions to $e^{-\Omega(\zeta^2)} \ll 1/r$, reliably preserving these heavy coordinates.
item.dc:creator: Lorenzo Beretta, Simone Bombari, Margalit Glasgow, Raphael Arkady Meyer, Kijun Shin, David P. Woodruff

item.title: Regev's Reduction Reaches Reconstruction
item.description: arXiv:2611.10283v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Regev's reduction uses a quantum Fourier transform to carry out reductions between various problems related to lattices and codes. We apply it to the problem of sampling from Gibbs distributions of certain classical spin glass Hamiltonians, which can equivalently be thought of as cost functions for average-case instances of an optimization problem called $D$-regular max-$k$-LINSAT. This problem becomes hard at low temperature. Here, we use a quantum decoding algorithm called Belief Propagation with Quantum Messages (BPQM) to solve the decoding problem arising from Regev's reduction. Our main contribution is a proof that the minimum temperature reachable using Regev+BPQM is exactly equal to the reconstruction threshold temperature for noisy channels transmitting signals on a tree network. This equality can be understood via Renes' duality between classical and quantum channels, which we use to show that quantum decoding is possible exactly when classical reconstruction on the dual problem is impossible. M{\'e}zard and Montanari identified this reconstruction temperature with a dynamical glass transition predicted by the one-step replica-symmetry breaking (1RSB) cavity equation. It is conjectured that local samplers such as Metropolis Monte Carlo and Glauber dynamics cannot equilibrate efficiently below this reconstruction temperature but may do so above it; our large numerical experiments show close agreement with this prediction across hundreds of different problem parameters. Therefore, our results rigorously show that Regev+BPQM reaches a temperature for which, to our knowledge, there is no matching classical guarantee, and brings Regev+BPQM to the conjectured limit of efficient Gibbs sampling by classical local dynamics.
item.dc:creator: Stephen P. Jordan, Quynh T. Nguyen, Leo Zhou

item.title: Sparse Predict and Demote: Optimal Scheduling with Minimal Size Advice
item.description: arXiv:2611.10293v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Knowledge of job sizes is crucial for optimizing the mean response time in single-server scheduling. However, predictions of job sizes are typically inexact and may be costly to obtain. Thus, a long-standing research question is: what is the minimal information about job sizes required to obtain near-optimal mean response time? We introduce a novel policy, \emph{Sparse Predict and Demote (SPD)}, and prove that it achieves order-optimal mean response time in heavy traffic while requiring only one-bit job-size predictions for a vanishing fraction of arrivals. SPD achieves heavy-traffic order-optimality even in situations when predictions are (i) inexact up to any fixed multiplicative error bound, and (ii) costly, i.e., the server is used to compute predictions and is thus unavailable to serve jobs while processing prediction queries. Finally, we use numerical experiments to illustrate that SPD maintains near-optimal performance beyond the heavy-traffic regime.
item.dc:creator: Chengyi Liu, Thodoris Lykouris, Junxuan Shen, Adam Wierman

item.title: A Simple Computer-Assisted Proof of the 5/6-Bound for Real-Period Pinwheel Scheduling
item.description: arXiv:2611.10624v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In pinwheel scheduling with real periods, an instance consists of $n$ tasks with real periods $1\le a_1\le a_2\le\cdots\le a_n$. The goal is to find a schedule that assigns one task to each day indefinitely such that, for every task $i\in\{1,\dots,n\}$ and every positive integer $\ell$, task $i$ occurs at least $\ell$ times in every block of $\lceil\ell a_i\rceil$ consecutive days. Given an instance $(a_1,a_2,\dots,a_n)$, its dimension is $n$, its density is $\sum_{i=1}^n1/a_i$, and its potential is $\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}1/a_i$. We prove that every real-valued instance of density at most 5/6 admits a periodic schedule of period length less than $4\cdot2^n$. For integer periods, the 5/6 density bound was a long-standing conjecture settled by Kawamura using a computer-assisted proof [STOC 2024, PNAS 2026]. Our result confirms the real-period conjecture of Fujiwara, Miyagi, and Ouchi [DMTCS 2026]. Our computer-assisted proof builds on Kawamura's ideas while using fewer explicit schedules. It combines dimension reduction by folding with nine satisfiability modulo theories (SMT) checks over linear real arithmetic. A set of 14287 explicit periodic schedules contains a schedule for every instance of dimension at most 8 and density at most 5/6, and for every instance of dimension 9 and potential at most 5/6. Folding is used to reduce every instance of larger dimension and potential at most 5/6 to an instance of dimension 9 and the same potential bound. We also prove that every real-valued instance with minimum period at least 4 and density at most 17/20=0.85 admits a periodic schedule of period length less than $19\cdot2^n$. The density bound 17/20 is tight and improves the 0.84-bound of Mishra, Rho, and Kleinberg [arXiv 2025] for integer periods. It also resolves the $a_1=4$ case of Kawamura's 2025 conjecture that integer-valued instances of density at most $1-(a_1-1)/(a_1(a_1+1))$ are schedulable.
item.dc:creator: Hiroshi Fujiwara, Grzegorz Gutowski, Katsuhisa Ouchi, Alexander Wolff

item.title: Parametrize Integer Programming by Packing Imbalanced Circuits
item.description: arXiv:2611.11046v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study the standard form Integer Programming problem (IP) parametrized by the imbalanced circuit packing number. This number is $0$ if and only if $A$ can be transformed to a totally unimodular matrix by row operations, in which case (IP) is solvable in polynomial time. We show that if the constraint matrix represents a graphic matroid, (IP) is fixed-parameter tractable when parametrized by the imbalanced circuit packing number of the matrix. The proof combines an Erd\H{o}s-P\'osa property for edge-colored non-monochromatic cycles with a reduction to mixed-integer programming using few integer variables. In contrast, by a reduction from the parity potential problem, we show NP-completeness of feasibility of (IP) when the constraint matrix represents a cographic matroid, even if kernel of the constraint matrix is $2$-regular and imbalanced circuits pairwise intersect.
item.dc:creator: Yuheng Shi

item.title: Sampling Colorings on $G(n, d/n)$ via Glauber Dynamics
item.description: arXiv:2611.12444v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study the mixing time of Glauber dynamics for sampling uniformly from the proper $q$-colorings of sparse Erd\H{o}s-R\'enyi random graphs $G(n,d/n)$. Our main result establishes that with probability $1-o(1)$ over the draw of $G$, Glauber dynamics is rapidly mixing for every $q\geq d+d^{1/2+\varepsilon}$, given any fixed $0<\varepsilon\leq1/2$ and any sufficiently large fixed $d$. In particular, the surplus of colors above $d$ is sublinear and close to $\sqrt{d}$. The achieved color range therefore approaches the tree uniqueness threshold and improves over the previously best achievable number of colors $q > 1.763 d$ due to Efthymiou, Hayes, Stefankovic, and Vigoda [SODA 2018]. Moreover, our mixing-time bound is $O(n^{2+o_d(1)})$, and hence almost quadratic as $d\rightarrow\infty$. Our proof is based on establishing a spectral gap for block dynamics resulting from a suitable decomposition of $G(n,d/n)$ into blocks and singleton vertices, ensuring that every high-degree vertex is encapsulated within a block. Our main technical contribution is a novel way of establishing rapid mixing of block dynamics via an integrated Bochner-Bakry-\'{E}mery approach, which we expect to have applications beyond sampling colorings. We further devise a new block decomposition of $G(n,d/n)$ that strengthens and simplifies similar constructions used in previous work. Finally, to compare block and Glauber dynamics, we establish a novel recursive separator decomposition of tree-like blocks, together with a coupling argument that avoids the need for nearly uniform color marginals at vertices adjacent to hubs. This comparison argument might be of independent interest.
item.dc:creator: Leon Schiller

item.title: Wolfe's Minimum-Norm-Point Method Generalizes the Simplex Method
item.description: arXiv:2611.12680v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Wolfe's method computes the point of minimum Euclidean norm in the convex hull of finitely many points. The method is parameterized by an insertion rule and it has been an open problem whether Wolfe's original rule guarantees a polynomial number of iterations (De Loera, Haddock, and Rademacher; STOC'18). We resolve this question by proving an exponential lower bound. In fact, we establish a tight connection to the simplex method for linear programming that allows us to transfer many lower bounds for simplex pivot rules to corresponding insertion rules of Wolfe's method. These include not only Wolfe's linopt rule via Dantzig's pivot rule, but also many other classical, randomized and history-based rules. As a corollary, we obtain the first exponential example for the Lawson-Hanson algorithm for nonnegative least squares, as well as PSPACE-hardness of deciding whether the linopt rule ever uses a given point.
item.dc:creator: Yann Disser, Nils Mosis

item.title: No Exponential Quantum Advantage for Decoded Quantum Interferometry with Local Quantum Decoders
item.description: arXiv:2611.12718v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Decoded quantum interferometry (DQI) reduces optimization of sparse linear constraint problems, and sampling from their Gibbs measures, to decoding a linear code from a quantum state. We study DQI on random $D$-regular $k$-sparse instances with $k\ge3$, for which local decoders such as belief propagation with quantum messages (BPQM) are commonly used. Such decoders estimate a typical codeword symbol using only the qudits within logarithmic distance of it. Our main insight is that the thresholds of the decoding problem induced by DQI correspond to phase transitions of the Gibbs measure that are well studied in statistical physics: tree reconstruction for local decoders and, for Max-$k$-XORSAT, condensation for the optimal decoder. This insight allows us to prove two main results. First, we prove an information-theoretic obstruction: no local decoder can recover the codeword with high probability above the tree reconstruction threshold. Conversely, we show that a decoder based on BPQM reaches this threshold. Since the cavity method predicts that local Markov chains equilibrate rapidly up to the same threshold, we expect DQI with local decoders to give no exponential speedup for sampling and no advantage in approximate optimization with amplitude functions that depend only on the number of violated constraints. Second, we consider the optimal decoder (the pretty-good measurement, for which no efficient implementation is known) and show that it succeeds exactly below the condensation threshold. The condensation threshold thus provides a tight upper bound on the performance of DQI with these amplitude functions, providing a strict refinement of the limit that Jordan et al.\ derived from the Holevo bound. Our results point to efficient nonlocal decoders that succeed between the two thresholds as the only viable path to a quantum advantage with DQI on these instances.
item.dc:creator: Brandon Augustino, Shouvanik Chakrabarti, Enrico Fontana, Dylan Herman, Guneykan Ozgul, Ruslan Shaydulin, Shreehari Sureshbabu, Jacob Watkins

item.title: Computing EF1 Allocations under Budget Constraints in Polynomial Time
item.description: arXiv:2611.12740v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study the fair allocation of indivisible items to agents with budget constraints and additive valuations. Each agent compares its own bundle with the subsets of another bundle that fit its budget. An allocation is envy-free up to one item (EF1) if, for every agent and every nonempty subset under comparison, removing an item of maximum value to that agent eliminates its envy. We require EF1 both between agents and towards the charity, which contains all unallocated items. EF1 allocations exist, but computing them in polynomial time has remained open even for homogeneous valuations. We resolve this problem with a polynomial-time algorithm for EF1 allocations under heterogeneous valuations. We also prove that detecting an EF1 violation is NP-complete. Equivalently, checking whether a given allocation is EF1 is coNP-complete. Finally, we give polynomial-time algorithms for envy-freeness up to any item (EFX) both when each agent's valuation is proportional to item size and when each agent has a fixed number of distinct positive item values. As an application, for homogeneous valuations and any $\varepsilon>0$, we obtain an EF1 allocation with at least a $(1/2-\varepsilon)$ fraction of the maximum social welfare in time polynomial in the input length and $1/\varepsilon$.
item.dc:creator: Tingwei Hu, Lili Mei, Guochuan Zhang

item.title: Learning Rate Decay Can Exponentially Accelerate SGD for Global Optimization of Nonconvex Functions
item.description: arXiv:2611.12769v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) is a workhorse algorithm for continuous optimization. It is a folk belief among deep learning practitioners that learning rate decay in SGD substantially improves performance. However, it has remained unclear whether learning rate decay offers an asymptotic advantage for global nonconvex optimization. We answer this question in the affirmative by demonstrating a natural class of nonconvex functions for which, we prove that SGD with learning rate decay requires exponentially fewer gradient queries for global optimization than SGD with any fixed learning rate in the small-step size regime. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first exponential advantage that has been demonstrated for learning rate decay. The class of functions we consider includes many popular benchmark nonconvex functions. Our results provide a robust explanatory theory for the empirically observed benefits of learning rate decay for global optimization. We show that annealing performs the non-logconcave sampling task associated to the optimization problem in polynomial time, via a novel application of weak Poincar\'{e} inequalities.
item.dc:creator: Guneykan Ozgul, Dylan Herman, Junhyung Lyle Kim, Shree Hari Sureshbabu, Shouvanik Chakrabarti

item.title: Balanced spanning forests of graphs: Hardness and solving methods
item.description: arXiv:2504.02421v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The balanced connected $k$-partition problem (\textsc{bcp}) is a classic problem, which consists in partitioning the set of vertices of a vertex-weighted connected graph into a collection of~$k$ classes such that each class induces a connected subgraph of \emph{roughly} the same weight. In this study, we investigate edge-weighted variants of $\textsc{bcp}$, where, given a connected graph $G$, a positive integer $k$, and edge weights, the goal is to compute a spanning $k$-forest~$\mathcal{T}$ of $G$ (i.e., a forest with exactly $k$ trees) that minimizes the weight of the heaviest tree in~$\mathcal{T}$ in the min-max version, or maximizes the weight of the lightest tree in~$\mathcal{T}$ in the max-min version. We show that both versions of this problem are $\NP$-hard on complete graphs with $k=2$, unweighted split graphs, and unweighted bipartite graphs with $k\geq 2$ fixed. Moreover, we prove that these problems do not admit subexponential-time algorithms, unless the Exponential-Time Hypothesis fails. We focus on the min-max version and devise a tight $k$-approximation algorithm, compact and non-compact integer {linear programming} formulations, branch-and-cut, and branch-and-price algorithms. Finally, we present the outcomes of an experimental study on the performance of different solution methods. The source code of the complete implementation of the proposed algorithms is also available.
item.dc:creator: Morteza Davari, Phablo F. S. Moura, Hande Yaman

item.title: The Trichotomy of Regular Property Testing
item.description: arXiv:2504.19152v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Property testing is concerned with the design of algorithms making a sublinear number of queries to distinguish whether the input satisfies a given property or is far from having this property. A seminal paper of Alon, Krivelevich, Newman, and Szegedy in 2001 introduced property testing of formal languages: the goal is to determine whether an input word belongs to a given language, or is far from any word in that language. They constructed the first property testing algorithm for the class of all regular languages. This opened a line of work with improved complexity results and applications to streaming algorithms. In this work, we show a trichotomy result: the class of regular languages can be divided into three classes, each associated with an optimal query complexity. Our analysis, which reasons directly and combinatorially on automata, yields effective characterizations of all three classes using so-called minimal blocking sequences.
item.dc:creator: Gabriel Bathie, Nathana\"el Fijalkow, Corto Mascle

item.title: Sublinear Time Quantum Sensitivity Sampling
item.description: arXiv:2509.16801v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We present a unified quantum sensitivity sampling framework that streamlines coreset construction for many classical approximation problems, significantly speeding up clustering, regression, and low-rank approximation. We assume $n,d\geq\mathrm{poly}(k/\epsilon)$ and, for regression, $n\geq\mathrm{poly}(d)$: - $k$-median/$k$-means: For $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^d$, we build an $\epsilon$-coreset of input points of size $\tilde O(k^{4/3}\epsilon^{-2})$ (resp. $\tilde O(k^{3/2}\epsilon^{-2})$) in time $\tilde O(\epsilon^{-1}n^{0.5}dk^{1.67})$ (resp. $\tilde O(\epsilon^{-1}n^{0.5}dk^{1.75})$). Our better $d$- and linear $1/\epsilon$-dependence improve on [Xue, Chen, Li and Jiang, ICML'23] for $d\geq\Omega(k^{7/3})$ (resp. $\Omega(k^{2.5})$). - $\ell_p$ regression: For $\min_x\|Ax-b\|_p$, $A\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d}$, we build an $\epsilon$-coreset of size $\tilde O_p(d^{\max\{1,p/2\}}\epsilon^{-2})$ in time $\tilde O_p(n^{0.5}d^{1.5}\epsilon^{-1})$ for $p\leq 2$ and $\tilde O_p(n^{0.5}d^{p/4+1}(\epsilon^{-1}+d^{0.5}))$ for $p>2$, matching [Liu and Ji, ICML'26] for $p\leq 2$ and improving on the prior best quantum sampling approach [Apers and Gribling, SICOMP'26] for all $p>2$. - Low-rank approximation: We give the first quantum sublinear-time algorithm for Frobenius-norm rank-$k$ approximation of $A\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times n}$ free of data-dependent parameters, running in $\tilde O(n^{0.5}dk^{0.5}\epsilon^{-0.5})$ time with factored output (plus $\tilde O(nk^2\epsilon^{-2})$ to materialize them). We also give sublinear algorithms for kernel and tensor variants. - Lower bound: For generic sensitivity sampling with total sensitivity $S$, any quantum algorithm outputting an $\epsilon$-coreset of size $o(\sqrt{nS})$ needs $\Omega(\sqrt{nS})$ queries, so our query complexity is optimal up to $\mathrm{poly}(\epsilon^{-1},\log n)$ and VC-dimension factors.
item.dc:creator: Zhao Song, David P. Woodruff, Lichen Zhang

item.title: Counting Hypertriangles through Hypergraph Orientations
item.description: arXiv:2601.03573v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Counting the number of small patterns is a central task in network analysis. While this problem is well studied for graphs, many real-world datasets are naturally modeled as hypergraphs, motivating the need for efficient hypergraph motif counting algorithms. In particular, we study the problem of counting hypertriangles - collections of three pairwise-intersecting hyperedges. These hypergraph patterns have a rich structure with multiple distinct intersection patterns unlike graph triangles. Inspired by classical graph algorithms based on orientations and degeneracy, we develop a new theoretical framework that generalizes these concepts to hypergraphs and yields provable algorithms for hypertriangle counting. We implement these ideas in DITCH (Degeneracy Inspired Triangle Counter for Hypergraphs) and show experimentally that it is faster on all but one small instance, achieving speedups of up to 100x, and is 6-100x more memory-efficient than existing state-of-the-art methods.
item.dc:creator: Daniel Paul-Pena, Vaishali Surianarayanan, Deeparnab Chakrabarty, C. Seshadhri

item.title: Catalytic Tree Evaluation From Matching Vectors
item.description: arXiv:2602.14320v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We give new algorithms for tree evaluation (S. Cook et al. TOCT 2012) in the catalytic-computing model (Buhrman et al. STOC 2014). Two existing approaches aim to solve tree evaluation (TreeEval) in low space: on the one hand, J. Cook and Mertz (STOC 2024) give an algorithm for TreeEval running in super-logarithmic space $O(\log n\log\log n)$ and super-polynomial time $n^{O(\log\log n)}$. On the other hand, an earlier algorithm of J. Cook and Mertz (STOC 2020), run on a catalytic tape, solves TreeEval in logarithmic $O(\log n)$ free space and polynomial time, but with polynomial $O(\sqrt{n})$ catalytic space. We show that the latter result can be improved. We give a catalytic algorithm for TreeEval with logarithmic $O(\log n)$ free space, polynomial runtime, and subpolynomial $2^{O(\log^\epsilon n)}$ catalytic space (for any $\epsilon > 0$). Our result also implies an improved simulation of time by catalytic space, via the reduction of Williams (STOC 2025). Our TreeEval algorithm comes from a framework, inspired by private information retrieval, that generically reduces tree evaluation to two combinatorial objects: matching-vector families and decoders (a new object we define that closely resembles decoding polynomials). These ingredients' parameters directly govern an algorithm's resources: the vectors' dimension determines its catalytic space, and the decoder's sparsity determines its free space and runtime. In addition to enabling our new algorithm, this framework explains existing tradeoffs, for example why the Cook-Mertz algorithm needs super-logarithmic space but no catalytic tape. It also lets better matching-vector families or decoders plug in directly to give better algorithms.
item.dc:creator: Alexandra Henzinger, Edward Pyne, Seyoon Ragavan

item.title: Transposition Is Nearly Optimal for IID List Update
item.description: arXiv:2603.10244v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The list update problem is one of the oldest and simplest problems in online algorithms: A set of items must be maintained in a list while requests to these items arrive over time. Whenever an item is requested, the algorithm pays a cost equal to the position of the item in the list. In the i.i.d. model, where requests are drawn independently from a fixed distribution, the static ordering by decreasing access probabilities $p_1\ge p_2\ge \dots \ge p_n$ achieves the minimal expected access cost $\mathrm{OPT}=\sum_{i=1}^n ip_i$. However, $p$ is typically unknown, and approximating it by tracking access frequencies creates undesirable overheads. A 50-year old conjecture by Rivest states that the Transposition rule (swap the requested item with its predecessor) is optimal among memoryless algorithms. While known to be false in the strict sense, prior research provided asymptotic confirmation of Rivest's conjecture for restricted distributions. We show that for all distributions, Transposition has stationary expected access cost at most $\mathrm{OPT}+1$, confirming Rivest's conjecture up to an unavoidable additive constant, and showing near-optimality even among algorithms with memory. More abstractly, it yields a purely memoryless procedure to approximately sort probabilities via sampling.
item.dc:creator: Christian Coester

item.title: Dimension-Free Sinkhorn for Optimal Transport: Bypassing Extremal Costs
item.description:
arXiv:2604.03787v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The Sinkhorn--Knopp (SK) algorithm is a cornerstone method for matrix scaling and entropically regularized optimal transport (EOT). Despite its empirical efficiency, existing bounds for achieving marginal accuracy $\varepsilon$ deteriorate severely in the presence of extreme entries, bottlenecked either by the global maximum regularized cost $\eta\|C\|_\infty$ (where $\eta$ is the regularization parameter and $C$ the cost matrix) or the matrix's minimum-to-maximum entry ratio $
u$. These bounds may be overly sensitive to rare extreme entries that do not dominate the overall matrix structure. We identify a broad structural regime in which the dependence on the magnitude of global extreme entries can be circumvented. For EOT, we introduce well-boundedness, a local mass property that captures the row- and column-wise bulk structure of the underlying matrix while maintaining robustness against scattered entrywise outliers. We prove that, governed by this structural condition, SK converges to the target transport plan for a problem of dimension $n$ in $O(\log n + \log(1/\varepsilon))$ iterations. This complexity bound is independent of the maximum regularized cost $\eta\|C\|_\infty$. A computationally negligible pre-scaling step eliminates this dimensional dependence, reducing the iteration complexity to a strictly dimension-free $O(\log(1/\varepsilon))$. Beyond EOT, we establish a sharp phase transition for general $( oldsymbol{u}, oldsymbol{v})$-scaling governed by a critical matrix density threshold. We prove that when a matrix's density exceeds this threshold, the iteration complexity is strictly independent of $
u$. Conversely, when the density falls below this threshold, the dependence on $
u$ becomes unavoidable; in this sub-critical regime, we construct instances where SK requires $\Omega(n/\varepsilon)$ iterations.
item.dc:creator: Kun He

item.title: On the Approximability of Max-Cut on 3-Colorable Graphs and Graphs with Large Independent Sets
item.description: arXiv:2604.10318v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Max-Cut is a classical graph-partitioning problem where given a graph $G = (V,E)$, the objective is to find a cut $(S,S^c)$ which maximizes the number of edges crossing the cut. In a seminal work, Goemans and Williamson gave an $\alpha_{GW} \approx 0.87856$-factor approximation algorithm for the problem, which was later shown to be tight by the work of Khot, Kindler, Mossel, and O'Donnell. Since then, there has been a steady progress in understanding the approximability at even finer levels, and a fundamental goal in this context is to understand how the structure of the underlying graph affects the approximability of the Max-Cut problem. In this work, we investigate this question by exploring how the chromatic structure of a graph affects the Max-Cut problem. While it is well-known that Max-Cut can be solved perfectly and near-perfectly in $2$-colorable and almost $2$-colorable graphs in polynomial time, here we explore its approximability under much weaker structural conditions such as when the graph is $3$-colorable or contains a large independent set. Our main contributions in this context are as follows: 1. We show Max-Cut is $\alpha_{GW}$-hard to approximate for $3$-colorable graphs. 2. We identify a natural threshold $\alpha^*$ such that the following holds. Firstly, for graphs which contain an independent set of size up to $\alpha^*$, Max-Cut continues to be $\alpha_{GW}$-factor hard to approximate. Furthermore, for any graph that contains an independent set of size $> \alpha^*$, there exists an efficient $>\alpha_{GW}$-approximation algorithm for Max-Cut. Our hardness results are derived using various analytical tools and novel variants of the Majority-Is-Stablest theorem, which might be of independent interest. Our algorithmic results are based on a novel SDP relaxation, which is then rounded and analyzed using interval arithmetic.
item.dc:creator: Suprovat Ghoshal, Neng Huang, Euiwoong Lee, Konstantin Makarychev, Yury Makarychev

item.title: Understanding Simulated Annealing: from Weak Poincar\'e Inequalities to a Discrete Optimal Transport Framework
item.description: arXiv:2605.05877v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Simulated annealing follows a path of distributions from an easy initial law to a target. Standard analyses require rapid mixing at every fixed temperature, which can fail for multimodal targets even when annealing succeeds. Motivated by the continuous optimal-transport analysis of annealed Langevin dynamics by Guo, Tao, and Chen (ICLR 2025), we develop a discrete optimal-transport framework for finite-state annealing.
