The discrete action of the path integrates the minimum electrical energy needed to route the demand $-\partial_s\pi_s$ through the chain's transition capacities. Like a path-dependent inverse conductance, it penalizes a bottleneck only when the path must move mass across it. We also introduce weak action, which leaves an $\varepsilon$ amount of this motion unrouted. Up to initialization error, action $\mathcal A$ gives reverse-KL error at most $\mathcal A/(4T)$ after $T$ expected updates, while weak action gives TV error at most $\varepsilon+\sqrt{\mathcal A^{w}_\varepsilon/(8T)}$. Paralleling canonical paths and Poincar\'e inequalities, we develop flow and spectral bounds, showing that pathwise (weak) Poincar\'e inequalities imply (weak) action bounds. We also show that a weak Poincar\'e inequality yields a genuine one after removing a small amount of mass. As a pathwise analogue of chain decomposition, we obtain a componentwise algorithm for mixtures with phase weights supplied at initialization. Applications include mean-field Ising and Potts models and bipartite spin systems. For every fixed $\delta>0$, we give a polynomial-time single-site annealing sampler for uniform independent sets in $(d,D)$-biregular bipartite graphs with $D/d\geq1+\delta$ and large $D$. To our knowledge, this is the first polynomial-time sampler requiring only a fixed multiplicative degree imbalance, strictly extending the $D\geq7d\log d$ regime of Cannon and Perkins (SODA 2020).
item.dc:creator: Yuchen He, Tianhui Jiang, Zhehan Lei, Sihan Wang, Chihao Zhang

item.title: Smoothed Score Queries and the Complexity of Sampling
item.description: arXiv:2605.27769v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study the query complexity of sampling from high-dimensional Gaussian distributions using gradient information. In the standard oracle model, exact gradients expose only matrix-vector products with the precision matrix, leading to polynomial approximation barriers and a characteristic $\sqrt{\kappa}$ dependence on the known spectral range. We show that this barrier disappears when the sampler is allowed to query smoothed scores, namely gradients of the logarithms of the Gaussian-convolved densities. For a centered Gaussian target with precision matrix $\Lambda$, a smoothed-score query at noise level $\tau$ gives access to the resolvent $(\Lambda+\tau^{-1}I)^{-1}$. Combining geometrically spaced noise levels with sinc-quadrature rational approximation, we obtain a sampler with $q=O((\log\kappa+\log(e\sqrt d/\delta_{\rm TV}))\log(e\sqrt d/\delta_{\rm TV}))$ smoothed-score queries for total variation error $\delta_{\rm TV}$, improving the condition-number dependence from $\sqrt{\kappa}$ to logarithmic. We also study finite-bit gradient oracles. Using coordinatewise quantization of the transformed smoothed-score answers and a final dithering step, we obtain a sampling scheme whose total communicated gradient information is polylogarithmic in $\kappa$; in particular, for fixed dimension and accuracy, the bit complexity is $O(\log^2\kappa)$. To complement these upper bounds, we introduce a channel-synthesis, or reverse-Shannon, converse technique for sampling lower bounds. This converts total-variation simulation guarantees into communication requirements and yields an $\Omega(d\log\kappa)$ bit lower bound for $d\ge2$ and fixed total variation error below one, as $\kappa\to\infty$. Together, these results identify smoothed scores as a provably more informative oracle for sampling and give nearly matching upper and lower bounds for its finite-bit complexity.
item.dc:creator: Jingbo Liu

item.title: Reducing Prize-Collecting Stroll and Related Routing Problems to Prize-Collecting TSP
item.description: arXiv:2606.18157v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We consider prize-collecting variants of the metric traveling salesperson problem (TSP). The prize-collecting stroll problem (PCS) is the path version of the prize-collecting TSP (PCTSP). Given a complete metric graph, two distinct prescribed terminal vertices $s,t$, and nonnegative penalties on vertices, PCS asks for an $s$-$t$ tour minimizing its length plus the total penalty of vertices that are not visited by it. We study a common generalization of PCTSP, PCS, and several related prize-collecting routing problems, which we call the prize-collecting $\Phi$-TSP. In this model, an interface $\Phi$ specifies a set of prescribed vertices together with their parity and connectivity requirements. We show that, if a polynomial-time $\rho$-approximation algorithm for PCTSP is available, then, for every fixed $\varepsilon>0$, there is a polynomial-time $(\rho+\varepsilon)$-approximation algorithm for the prize-collecting $\Phi$-TSP when the number of prescribed vertices is bounded by a fixed constant. Consequently, PCS can be approximated as well as PCTSP up to an arbitrarily small additive loss, closing the gap between the best-known approximation guarantees for the two problems.
item.dc:creator: Hong Li

item.title: Hadamard Flattening and Gaussian Pooling Sketch for Least Squares with Coordinate-wise Guarantee
item.description: arXiv:2608.26552v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Randomized sketch-and-solve algorithms accelerate overconstrained $\ell_2$ regression by replacing the input with a much smaller, randomly projected problem. While standard subspace embeddings nearly preserve the regression cost, coordinate-wise accuracy is more delicate: rather than the objective value, we want the solution vector itself to be close to the optimum in $\ell_\infty$ norm. Specifically, we seek $x'\in\mathbb{R}^d$ with $\|x'-x^\star\|_\infty\leq\frac{\epsilon}{\sqrt d}\|Ax^\star-b\|_2\|A^\dagger\|_{\mathrm{op}}$, where $A\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d}$ is the design matrix, $b\in\mathbb{R}^n$ the label vector, $x^\star$ the optimal solution and $A^\dagger$ the pseudo-inverse of $A$. Price, Song and Woodruff introduced this problem and claimed that the subsampled randomized Hadamard transform (SRHT) with $O(\epsilon^{-2}d^{1+\Theta(\sqrt{\log\log n/\log d})})$ rows achieves this guarantee; we point out a gap in the proof. Song, Ye, Yin and Zhang later claimed $O(\epsilon^{-2}d\log^3 n)$ rows, but their proof relies on an independence assumption that does not hold in general, and we exhibit an explicit instance on which it fails. To achieve a truly nearly-linear-in-$d$ row count, we introduce a new fast, dense randomized transform combining a randomized Hadamard flattening, a random permutation, and balanced, disjoint Gaussian pooling. Conditioned on the Hadamard-and-permutation stage, the sketched problem becomes an exact Gaussian regression whose noise is independent of the entire sketched design, exactly what Song, Ye, Yin and Zhang's argument was missing. Our sketch yields the $\ell_\infty$ guarantee with $m=O(\epsilon^{-2}d\log d)$ rows, using one Hadamard pass with padded internal dimension $N=\widetilde{O}(n+\epsilon^{-2}d^3)$. It is also efficient to apply: $(SA,Sb)$ can be computed in $O(Nd\log N)=\widetilde{O}(nd+\epsilon^{-2}d^4)$ time.
item.dc:creator: Zhao Song, Lichen Zhang

item.title: Fast Odd-Permutation Sums in Characteristic Two and Shortest Even Directed Cycles
item.description: arXiv:2609.12021v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: For an $n\times n$ matrix over a field of characteristic two, let $\Phi$ denote the sum of the odd permutation monomials. We give a deterministic algorithm that evaluates $\Phi$ and all its first partial derivatives using $O(n^\omega)$ field operations, where $2<\omega\le3$ is any fixed admissible exponent for square matrix multiplication. As an application, we obtain faster randomized algorithms for shortest even directed cycles. Given an $n$-vertex directed graph whose shortest even cycle has length $\ell$, with high probability we compute $\ell$ and the union of the arcs of all shortest even cycles in $\widetilde O(n^\omega\ell)$ time, and find one such cycle in $\widetilde O(n^\omega\ell+n^2\ell^2)$ time. The resulting general bounds are $\widetilde O(n^{\omega+1})$ and $\widetilde O(n^4)$, respectively, improving on the $\widetilde O(n^{\omega+3})$ and $\widetilde O(n^{\omega+4})$ bounds of Bj\"orklund, Husfeldt, and Kaski [BHK24].
item.dc:creator: Boxuan Chen (Peking University), Bin Cui (Peking University), Hanqing Li (Peking University), Xupeng Miao (Peking University), Haoze Wang (Unaffiliated)

item.title: Pseudometric-Weighted Correlation Clustering via Spectral Preclustering
item.description: arXiv:2609.17403v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study \emph{pseudometric-weighted correlation clustering}, in which pairs have arbitrary positive or negative labels and nonnegative disagreement weights satisfying the triangle inequality. For every fixed $\varepsilon>0$, we give a randomized polynomial-time $(2+\varepsilon)$-approximation, improving the previous factor of $10/3$. The algorithm constructs an explicit feasible solution to the cluster LP with polynomial support and value at most $(1+\varepsilon)\mathrm{OPT}$, where $\mathrm{OPT}$ is the minimum integral clustering cost. Our main contribution is a weighted preclustering construction that witnesses a near-optimal clustering while bounding the total weight of admissible edges by $\operatorname{poly}(1/\varepsilon)\mathrm{OPT}$. We obtain admissibility certificates from random walks, where the factor-two Ptolemy's inequality for pseudometrics reduces the required length of walks from $O(\log n)$ to a constant. We then bound the rounding error separately at each vertex and use the triangle inequality to control its weighted cost. Sampling and coverage corrections produce an exactly feasible solution, and the factor-two rounding completes the approximation algorithm.
item.dc:creator: Chenglin Fan, Dahoon Lee, Euiwoong Lee

item.title: Single-Exponential Algorithms for Directed Feedback Vertex Set on Planar Digraphs
item.description: arXiv:2609.32728v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We consider Directed Feedback Vertex Set on planar digraphs, parameterized by the solution size $k$. We give a randomized algorithm with one-sided error running in time $(2+\sqrt5)^k n^{O(1)}= 4.24^k n^{O(1)}$, and a deterministic algorithm running in time $8.04^k n^{O(1)}$. Both algorithms use polynomial space. To the best of our knowledge, these are the first single-exponential fixed-parameter algorithms for Directed Feedback Vertex Set on planar digraphs. This contrasts with general digraphs, where the best known algorithms run in time $2^{O(k\log k)}(n+m)$, and whether a $2^{o(k\log k)}n^{O(1)}$-time algorithm exists remains a major open problem. Our main tool is an exact Euler-type counting identity for plane digraphs. It shows that every small solution must carry a large share of the vertices whose in- and out-arcs alternate in the embedding, while solutions avoiding such vertices can be computed by reducing to Directed Feedback Arc Set, which is known to be solvable in polynomial time on planar digraphs via the Lucchesi-Younger theorem.
item.dc:creator: Daniel Lokshtanov, Saket Saurabh, Jie Xue

item.title: Partially Dynamic Single-Source Shortest Paths in Almost-Linear Time
item.description: arXiv:2610.07468v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study $(1+\epsilon)$-approximate single-source distances in directed graphs with positive integer edge weights in $[1,W]$. For every $0<\epsilon\le1$, we give deterministic data structures for either edge insertions or edge deletions with total update time $m^{1+o(1)}\epsilon^{-1}\log W$, where $m\ge n$ bounds the total number of initially present and inserted edges. Both structures explicitly maintain approximate distance estimates, answer distance queries in constant time, and identify unreachable vertices exactly. The incremental structure additionally reports a simple $(1+\epsilon)$-approximate source path $P$ in $O(|P|)$ time. Our decremental structure gives the first almost-linear-time algorithm. It improves the previous best randomized expected bound of $\widetilde O(\min\{n^2,mn^{2/3}\})$ against an oblivious adversary [BPW20]. Our incremental bound improves the $\epsilon^{-B}$ dependence of the $B$-level recursive algorithm of [Liu26] to an explicit $\epsilon^{-1}$ factor while retaining almost-linear dependence on $m$. Our algorithms use modified interior point methods. For edge deletions, we extend the single-pair distance framework of [vBCKLMPSS24] to all targets simultaneously. A shared potential and one dynamic minimum-ratio cut instance support global updates to the distance labels. Our main insight is that constant relative cut balance certifies approximate distances at every target. For edge insertions, we develop an analogous circulation-based formulation implemented through the dynamic minimum-ratio cycle structure of [CKLMP24]. We also give a black-box reduction from distance estimates to path reporting in incremental graphs, with $m^{1+o(1)}\epsilon^{-1}\log W$ additional maintenance time. This reduction may be of independent interest.
item.dc:creator: Bin Cui (Peking University), Hanqing Li (Peking University), Xupeng Miao (Peking University), Haoze Wang (Unaffiliated)

item.title: Taxonomic Classification with Tag Arrays
item.description: arXiv:2610.10500v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We present a tool, KATKA, for taxonomic classification with tag arrays. Compared to Ahmed et al.'s state-of-the-art tool Cliffy ({\it Genome Research}, 2025) on the SILVA dataset from their paper and a readset similar to one of theirs, KATKA is faster, more accurate, much smaller and drastically easier to build.
item.dc:creator: Travis Gagie, Gonzalo Navarro

item.title: Online Interval Selection with Binary Predictions: Optimal Consistency and a Continuous Robustness Tradeoff
item.description: arXiv:2610.37361v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study online interval selection with binary predictions of membership in a final optimal solution. Requests arrive in arbitrary order; accepted requests may be revoked, but rejected or revoked requests cannot be recovered. With rewards proportional to interval length, the best consistency under finite strict robustness is $d=(3+\sqrt5)/2$ when both guarantees hold almost surely on each fixed input, including for randomized algorithms. A continuous lower bound forces consistency strictly above $d$ at every robustness budget below $4\varphi+3\approx9.472$, whereas our deterministic algorithm attains $d$ with exact robustness $\varphi^5\approx11.090$, where $\varphi=(1+\sqrt5)/2$. Each held interval inherits a ledger recording positive prediction mass lost through irrevocable decisions. Tuning the replacement costs and both special thresholds gives a continuous family with exact consistency throughout and exact robustness on two parameter intervals, including $(C,R)=(25/9,10)$ and $(4,7)$. Randomization permits expected consistency approaching one with finite expected robustness, whereas almost-sure robustness forces expected consistency strictly above two at every finite budget.
item.dc:creator: Zhong Han

item.title: Tight Asymptotic Bounds on the Size of Order Graphs
item.description: arXiv:2610.39311v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Order graphs were introduced by Arroyuelo et al.\ (TODS 2024) as a generalization of the ring index, to support worst-case optimal joins on relations of arity $d$ while storing few columns: the index stores one column per edge, so its size is proportional to the number of edges of an order graph. It was known that the minimum number of edges lies between $\Omega(2^d\sqrt d)$ and $O(2^d d)$, and the lower bound had been claimed to be $42$ for $d=6$. We first exhibit an optimal order graph with only $40$ edges for $d=6$, and show that the proof of that lower bound holds only for unions of cycles, whereas order graphs can be smaller than the smallest set of cycles. We give a corrected statement and proof that holds for every order graph: there must be at least $\max_m\binom dm\lceil m/2\rceil$ edges. This bound is $40$ (hence tight) for $d=6$. We then settle the asymptotic question: the minimum size is $\Theta(2^d\sqrt d)$. This is obtained via an explicit construction, based on symmetric chain decompositions of the Boolean lattice, with at most $(d-1)\binom{d}{\lfloor d/2\rfloor}+2^d$ edges. The upper bound is within a factor $4+O(d^{-1/2})$ of the lower bound, and both numerically and asymptotically better than trie switching. Finally, we cast the problem as a set cover with connectivity constraints, which yields an exact ILP formulation and a greedy heuristic. With them we find optimal order graphs for $d\le 6$ in the bidirectional and for $d \le 7$ in the unidirectional model, showing that our lower bounds are tight there, and improve the best known order graphs for $d=7$ and $8$.
item.dc:creator: Ruben Becker, Adri\'an G\'omez-Brand\'on, Gonzalo Navarro, Nicola Prezza

item.title: Ranking and Unranking Permutations in Heap's Order
item.description: arXiv:2611.05397v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Heap's algorithm is a permutation generation method with very low constant overhead. Its element-interchanging mechanism, however, prevents the standard factorial-base Lehmer code from being applied directly, and to our knowledge no explicit Rank/Unrank algorithm for the Heap order has been published. This paper describes the block structure of Heap's algorithm in terms of rearrangement operators: the net effect of a block-internal traversal is a tail-preserving operator and the block-boundary swap is a top-level swap operator, and together they yield a closed-form recurrence for the block transitions. On this basis a bottom-up Unrank algorithm and a top-down Rank algorithm are built from one and the same closed-form in-block mapping; both run in $O(n^3)$ time and $O(n)$ space and require no factorial-scale precomputed table. The supporting proofs use a synchronized strong induction on the dimension to establish the bijectivity of the trailing-element mapping, closed forms for the final arrangement and for the trailing sequence, the dichotomy of its cycle structure, and the reciprocity of Rank and Unrank. The Heap order is in fact the colex order of the mixed-radix code.
item.dc:creator: Yusheng Hu

item.title: GreedTok Is a 0.3287-Approximation for Tokenization, Within 3% of the Best Possible Constant
item.description: arXiv:2611.07346v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A tokenizer's vocabulary is chosen once and used on every input, so it matters how much compression a greedy vocabulary can lose. GreedTok (Lim et al., 2025) picks $k$ tokens one at a time, each time the string that saves the most tokens; its worst-case ratio was open. We prove that GreedTok saves at least 0.3287 of the optimal number of tokens saved, on every corpus and budget, while junction corpora show that no constant above 0.3387 is possible. The lower-bound proof is written out in full and uses no computer certificates. Its key idea is to track the order of greedy's choices: given that order, the pattern greedy leaves inside an optimal token depends on two numbers, and an induction peels off one chosen string at a time; without the order, a needed inequality fails for a 20-character token. Over 256 symbols, GreedTok's ratio exceeds 0.33861 for every $k\ge 104{,}910$, and over $k^c$ symbols with $c<1/2$ it is at least 0.4386 in the limit. We also show that the objective is APX-hard: it has no PTAS unless P = NP.
item.dc:creator: Kundan Baliga, Aiden Xie, Aditya Byju

item.title: Greedy Byte-Pair Encoding Achieves 0.391 of the Optimum, Past the One-Third Barrier for Packing-Based Analyses
item.description: arXiv:2611.08671v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE) builds most language-model tokenisers by repeatedly merging a most frequent adjacent pair of symbols. How much shortening can this greedy rule lose against the best $k$ merges? Kozma and Voderholzer proved that greedy achieves at least one third of the optimal shortening; the best known upper bound is $(1-e^{-2})/2\approx 0.432$. We show that one third is a barrier for packing-based analyses, which see the optimum only through a pair packing, and we prove that greedy achieves at least $0.391$ of the optimum on every input, with any tie-breaking. The key idea is rule determinism: all copies of a rule of the optimum spell the same letters, so when one greedy replacement destroys three of the optimum's merge points, half a unit can be refunded on each side. A weaker bound, $0.374$, has a short proof that needs no computer; $0.391$ adds a certificate in exact arithmetic. We also show that the worst-case ratio is exactly $3/4$ for two merges and at most $7/12$ for three.
item.dc:creator: Kundan Baliga, Aiden Xie, Aditya Byju

item.title: Smoothed Analysis of Nash Equilibrium and Fixed Point Computation, and Efficiency of the Homotopy Method
item.description: arXiv:2501.10884v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study, under a smoothed analysis perspective, the complexity of three PPAD-complete problems: computing Nash equilibria, computing fixed points, and solving variational inequalities. We consider a general perturbation model that bounds the probability density of the quantities evaluated by our algorithms. As special cases, it captures worst-case games perturbed by small random per-action costs, and worst-case maps perturbed by a small random affine function. Under these models, we show that classical algorithmic paradigms, cover-based search and homotopy path-following provably outperform the worst-case state-of-the-art. For games with a constant number of players and $n$ strategies per player, a recursive cover-based algorithm computes an $\varepsilon$-Nash equilibrium using $\log(1/\varepsilon)\cdot 2^{O(n)}$ expected payoff-vector computations, compared to the worst-case runtime tradeoffs of $\log(1/\varepsilon)\cdot n^{O(n)}$, $(1/\varepsilon)^{O(n)}$, $2^{O(\log^2 n/\varepsilon^2)}$, and $2^{O(n)}\mathrm{poly}(\log(1/\varepsilon))$. For fixed points and variational inequalities of bounded and Lipschitz maps on the $n$-dimensional $\ell_2$ unit ball, the same approach runs in expected time $\log(1/\varepsilon)\cdot 2^{O(n)}$, compared to the worst-case $(1/\varepsilon)^{O(n)}$; the $2^{\Omega(n)}$ factor is necessary by prior work [Rubinstein, 2017]. For general smooth maps, we further analyze the classical predictor--corrector homotopy method, for which only qualitative convergence guarantees were previously known, showing that under perturbations the homotopy path is well conditioned and has length $2^{O(n)}$, so that the method finds an $\varepsilon$-approximate solution in time $2^{O(n)}\cdot\mathrm{poly}(1/p)/\varepsilon$ with probability at least $1-p$.
item.dc:creator: Idan Attias, Yuval Dagan, Constantinos Daskalakis, Rui Yao, Manolis Zampetakis

item.title: Private Continual Counting of Unbounded Streams
item.description: arXiv:2506.15018v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study the problem of differentially private continual counting in the unbounded setting where the input size $n$ is not known in advance. Current state-of-the-art algorithms based on optimal instantiations of the matrix mechanism cannot be directly applied here because their privacy guarantees only hold when key parameters are tuned to $n$. Using the common `doubling trick' avoids knowledge of $n$ but leads to suboptimal and non-smooth error. We solve this problem by introducing novel matrix factorizations based on logarithmic perturbations of the function $\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-z}}$ studied in prior works, which may be of independent interest. The resulting algorithm has smooth error, and for any $\alpha > 0$ and $t\leq n$, it is able to privately estimate the sum of the first $t$ data points with $O(\log^{2}(t)(\log\log t)^{1+2\alpha})$ variance. It requires $O(t)$ space and amortized $O(\log t)$ time per round, compared to $O(\log(n)\log(t))$ variance, $O(n)$ space and $O(n \log n)$ pre-processing time for the nearly-optimal bounded-input algorithm of Henzinger et al. Empirically, we find that our algorithm's performance is also comparable to theirs in absolute terms: with optimized parameters, our variance is less than $2\times$ theirs for $t$ as large as $2^{32}$.
item.dc:creator: Ben Jacobsen, Kassem Fawaz

item.title: Induced Cycles of Many Lengths
item.description: arXiv:2602.06874v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Let $G$ be a graph and let $\mathrm{cl}(G)$ be the number of distinct induced cycle lengths in $G$. We show that for $c,t\in \mathbb N$, every graph $G$ that does not contain an induced subgraph isomorphic to $K_{t+1}$ or $K_{t,t}$ and satisfies $\mathrm{cl}(G) \le c$ has bounded treewidth. As a consequence, we obtain a polynomial-time algorithm for deciding whether a graph $G$ contains induced cycles of at least three distinct lengths.
item.dc:creator: Maria Chudnovsky, Ilya Maier

item.title: Efficient Adaptive Data Analysis over Dense Distributions
item.description: arXiv:2602.07732v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Modern data workflows are inherently adaptive, repeatedly querying the same dataset to refine and validate sequential decisions, but such adaptivity can lead to overfitting and invalid statistical inference. Adaptive Data Analysis (ADA) mechanisms address this challenge; however, there is a fundamental tension between computational efficiency and sample complexity. For $T$ rounds of adaptive analysis, computationally efficient algorithms typically incur suboptimal $O(\sqrt{T})$ sample complexity, whereas for arbitrary distributions, algorithms with $O(\log T)$ sample complexity are computationally intractable under standard cryptographic assumptions. In this work, we shed light on this trade-off by identifying a natural class of data distributions under which both computational efficiency and logarithmic sample complexity in $T$ are achievable. We propose a computationally efficient ADA mechanism that attains $O(\log T)$ sample complexity, optimal in its dependence on $T$, when the data distribution is dense with respect to a known prior. This setting includes, in particular, feature-label data distributions arising in distribution-specific learning. As a consequence, our mechanism also yields a sample-efficient (i.e., $O(\log T)$ samples) statistical query oracle in the distribution-specific setting. Moreover, although our algorithm is not based on differential privacy, it satisfies a relaxed privacy notion known as Predicate Singling Out (PSO) security (Cohen and Nissim 2020) whenever the number of its possible update transcripts is polynomial in the sample size. Our results thus reveal an inherent connection between adaptive data analysis and privacy beyond differential privacy.
item.dc:creator: Joon Suk Huh

item.title: DASHQuant: Provable Quantization with a Single Randomized Hadamard Transform
item.description: arXiv:2605.13810v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Vector quantization via random projection followed by scalar quantization is a fundamental primitive in machine learning, with applications ranging from similarity search to federated learning and KV cache compression. While dense random rotations yield clean theoretical guarantees, they require $\Theta(d^2)$ time. The randomized Hadamard transform $HD$ reduces this cost to $O(d \log d)$, but its discrete structure complicates analysis and leads to weaker or purely empirical compression guarantees. In this work, we introduce DASHQuant (Dithered Accelerated Single-Hadamard Quantization), a provable variant of this approach. Specifically, the quantizer applies $HD$ to the input vector and adds a random dithering before quantizing, injecting additional randomness at negligible cost. We prove that this approach is unbiased and provides mean squared error bounds that asymptotically match those achievable with truly random rotation matrices. In particular, we prove that a dithered version of TurboQuant, and a special case of EDEN, achieves mean squared error $\bigl(\pi\sqrt{3}/2 + o(1)\bigr) \cdot 4^{-b}$ at $b$ bits per coordinate, where the $o(1)$ term vanishes uniformly over all unit vectors and all dimensions as the number of quantization levels grows.
item.dc:creator: Ying Feng, Piotr Indyk, Michael Kapralov, Dmitry Krachun, Boris Prokhorov

item.title: Lumberjack: Better Differentially Private Random Forests through Heavy Hitter Detection in Trees
item.description: arXiv:2605.22756v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Random forests are widely used in fields involving sensitive tabular data, but existing approaches to enforcing differential privacy (DP) typically degrade performance to the point of impracticality. In this paper, we introduce Lumberjack, a differentially private random forest algorithm that achieves substantially higher utility by constructing large random decision trees and then applying aggressive, privacy-preserving pruning to retain only sufficiently populated nodes. A key component of our approach is a novel $(\varepsilon,\delta)$-DP heavy hitter detection algorithm for hierarchical data, whose error is $O_{\varepsilon,\delta}(\sqrt{\log h})$ for trees of height $h$ and may be of independent interest. This favorable scaling enables the use of significantly deeper trees than in prior work, leading to improved expressiveness under privacy constraints. Our empirical evaluation on benchmark datasets shows that Lumberjack consistently outperforms prior DP random forest methods, establishing a new state of the art. In particular, our approach yields substantial improvements in the privacy-utility trade-off for practical privacy budgets. Our findings suggest that carefully designed DP random forests can close much of the utility gap, highlighting a promising and underexplored direction for future research.
item.dc:creator: Christian Janos Lebeda, David Erb, Tudor Cebere, Aur\'elien Bellet

item.title: Express Language Modeling
item.description: arXiv:2606.10944v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We introduce a new tool, Express, for converting a non-causal attention approximation into a causal approximation with matching approximation guarantees. When combined with the state-of-the-art Thinformer approximation, Express improves upon the best known causal attention guarantees, delivering $\log^{3/2}(n)/s$ approximation error with only $O(s)$ memory and $O(s^2 \log^2(n))$ compression overhead for a sequence of length $n$. We pair these developments with an efficient I/O-aware Triton implementation, demonstrate substantial speedups over FlashAttention 2, and use Express to overcome four resource bottlenecks in the language modeling pipeline: long-context prefill, KV cache compression, long-form memory-constrained decoding, and long-form compute-constrained decoding.
item.dc:creator: Albert Gong, Annabelle Michael Carrell, Raaz Dwivedi, Lester Mackey

item.title: List coloring uncrowded hypergraphs at the shattering threshold
item.description: arXiv:2606.18048v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: A foundational theorem of Ajtai, Koml\'os, Pintz, Spencer, and Szemer\'edi asserts that every $n$-vertex $k$-uniform uncrowded hypergraph (i.e., with girth at least $5$) of maximum degree at most $\Delta$ contains an independent set of size $cn(\log\Delta/\Delta)^{\frac{1}{k-1}}$ for some absolute constant $c>0$. Improving an earlier bound of Frieze and Mubayi, Iliopoulos showed that every such hypergraph has list chromatic number at most $(1+o(1))(k-1)(\Delta/\log\Delta)^{\frac{1}{k-1}}$. Determining the optimal leading constant in this bound remains a major open problem. A natural target, suggested by the coupon-collector heuristic, is $(k-1)^{\frac{1}{k-1}}$, which also corresponds to the shattering threshold for coloring sparse random hypergraphs. Our main result shows that this target is attained: for every integer $k\ge2$, every $k$-uniform uncrowded hypergraph of maximum degree at most $\Delta$ satisfies: $$\chi_\ell(\mathcal{H})\le(1+o(1))\Big((k-1)\frac{\Delta}{\log\Delta}\Big)^{\frac{1}{k-1}}.$$ In particular, this confirms a 2019 conjecture of Molloy for uncrowded hypergraphs. Building on this result, we prove that every $k$-uniform linear hypergraph of maximum degree at most $\Delta$ has chromatic number at most $(c_k+o(1))(\Delta/\log\Delta)^{\frac{1}{k-1}}$, where $c_k\to1$ as $k\to\infty$, thereby proving a conjecture of Verstra\"ete and Wilson on the independence number of linear hypergraphs in the stronger form of colorings. Our techniques also yield a palette sparsification theorem for uncrowded hypergraphs, partially answering a question of Casselgren and Eriksson.
item.dc:creator: Abhishek Dhawan, Abhishek Methuku, Minh-Quan Vo

item.title: The Existence of Maximin Share Allocations is $\Delta_2^P$-complete
item.description: arXiv:2609.15841v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The maximin share (MMS) guarantee has become one of the central fairness benchmarks for allocating indivisible items. Since Kurokawa, Procaccia, and Wang [EC'14, JACM'18] showed that exact MMS allocations need not exist, a substantial literature has developed around the existence and computation of approximate MMS allocations, including the recent work of Heidari, Kaviani, Seddighin, and Shahrezaei [SODA'26]. In contrast, a fundamental complexity question posed more than a decade ago by Bouveret and Lema\^itre [JAAMAS'16] has remained unresolved: how hard is it to decide whether an exact MMS allocation exists? For additive valuations, Lonc and Truszczynski [JAIR'20] established membership in the complexity class $\Delta_2^P$ (also known as $P^{NP}$), but no hardness result was known. For the more general class of 2-additive valuations, Bouveret and Lema\^itre established NP-hardness, leaving a substantial gap to the $\Delta_2^P$ upper bound. Moreover, the complexity of MMS existence for additive and $k$-additive valuations was posed as open questions. We resolve this longstanding question by proving that deciding the existence of an MMS allocation for additive goods is $\Delta_2^P$-complete, even for five agents. Additionally, we prove weak coNP-hardness for three agents, thereby establishing a precise dichotomy with the known existence guarantee for two agents, and strong coNP-hardness when the number of agents is unrestricted. Furthermore, our strong hardness construction yields an inverse-polynomial gap in the optimal MMS approximation ratio, ruling out an FPTAS for approximating this ratio unless P=NP. Finally, we show that all these results for goods extend to the chores setting through a polynomial-time transformation that preserves MMS existence.
item.dc:creator: Sushmita Gupta, Sanjay Seetharaman

item.title: Query-Optimal and Gate-Efficient Lindbladian Simulation
item.description: arXiv:2609.18757v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We give a quantum algorithm for Lindbladian simulation given a block encoding of the Hamiltonian $H$ and a projected unitary encoding of the stacked jump operator $B=\sum_{k=1}^m \lvert k\rangle\otimes L_k$, with normalization factors $\alpha_H$ and $\alpha_B$, respectively. For evolution time $t$, set $\tau=(\alpha_H+\alpha_B^2)t$. The algorithm approximates the evolution channel to diamond-norm error $\varepsilon$ using $O\!\left(\tau+\frac{\log(1/\varepsilon)}{\log\!\left(e+\log(1/\varepsilon)/\tau\right)}\right)$ oracle queries, matching the query lower bound for Hamiltonian simulation. The number of additional one- and two-qubit gates is linear in the query complexity up to polylogarithmic factors. The query- and gate-complexity bounds extend to Lipschitz-continuous time-dependent Lindbladians under coherent time-indexed oracle access. Our construction uses a one-query transducer that implements a product of rational approximations to short-time evolution when supplied with a catalyst. We bound the error from omitting the catalyst by exploiting orthogonality between different sequences of Kraus labels. The gate implementation combines a compressed Kraus-label representation, which stores only the positions and values of the nonzero labels, with the rotation factorization of Chen et al.
item.dc:creator: Boyang Chen, Minbo Gao, Xinzhao Wang, Shuo Zhou

item.title: Do Language Models Know Which Constraints Belong Together?
item.description: arXiv:2611.05726v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Dantzig-Wolfe reformulation strengthens the linear relaxation of a mixed-integer program by convexifying a chosen set of constraint families, and every candidate costs a column generation run. The choice is hard when families strengthen the bound only together; the classical inequalities of lot sizing, network design and facility location rest on such zero-marginal groups. We prove that when each evaluation convexifies at most $s$ of $k$ families, any method that observes only bounds needs a covering number of evaluations, of order $k^w$, to find a hidden group of $w$ families. A prediction that misses $e$ members reduces the cost to $\Theta(k^e)$ by a staged search, so the evaluations a prediction saves measure what the predictor knows. We study two sources of predictions: a lookahead at an optimal LP dual, blind to groups whose families share no variable, and a language model that reads the model, which JointDW verifies with the staged search and interleaves with the lookahead at a bounded loss. Zero-marginal groups appear in three of ten MIPLIB-NL models with an improvable bound and in all 59 standard lot-sizing, network-design and facility-location instances, where GCG's detector convexifies a set with no gain on 38 of them. On MIPLIB-NL the strongest language models find the groups about as often as the lookahead, and on textbook models their predictions rest on the names. Given every coefficient of a larger model, one reasoning model names the classical group in all but one answer, also with the names permuted or removed, and needs fewer evaluations than the lookahead for pairs of families; a predictor trained on the same class matches this only after hundreds of labeled evaluations. On the benchmark instances the language models name the best pair more often than the lookahead and the detector, and the sets of GPT-6.1 Sol come closest to the branch-and-price time of the best set.
item.dc:creator: Junbo Jacob Lian, Kaixuan Chen, Hanzhang Qin, Huiling Chen, Chaoyu Zhang, Chung-Piaw Teo
